templates.title: Job SLA misses with retries and repair runs
templates.subtopic: date spines, latest-per-group, interval arithmetic, outer joins

sections.scenario: A platform team runs scheduled data jobs (ingestion, transformations, feature refreshes) on a lakehouse. Each job produces the output for one logical date, its run_date. A run can fail and be retried automatically, and an engineer can start a repair run later, sometimes the next day, sometimes after a run already succeeded because the output was wrong. Downstream teams want one honest daily report: did each job deliver each date's output by its SLA?
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns run_date, job_id, runs, deadline, delivered_at, status, minutes_late: one row per job and per date from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}} on which the job has a schedule in effect, ordered by run_date, job_id. The deadline is run_date plus the schedule's schedule_time (UTC) plus sla_minutes; it can fall on the next day. runs counts every row in job_runs for that job and run_date, whatever its type or state. A later successful run replaces the output, so the date's output is final when its latest successful run ends (the largest end_ts among runs with result_state = 'SUCCESS'): that time is delivered_at, or NULL if no run succeeded. status is MET if delivered_at is at or before the deadline, LATE if after it, MISSED if NULL. minutes_late is 0 for MET, the number of minutes after the deadline rounded up to a whole minute for LATE, and NULL for MISSED. {{schedule_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A run belongs to its run_date, not to the date it started or ended. The sample has {{runs}} runs.
sections.assumptions: Job names, schedules, SLAs and durations are hypothetical. "The latest successful run defines delivery" is this exercise's rule for jobs whose outputs are overwritten by repairs; check your own platform's semantics before reusing it.
sections.criteria: Report grain built from the window and the schedules, not from runs alone (Very Hard); runs attached by run_date; latest success defines delivery while failed repairs do not; deadline arithmetic across midnight in UTC; inclusive deadline; rounding up; the schedule in effect on each date (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss restatements, local time zones and incremental refresh.

clarifications.q: A repair run for Monday starts on Tuesday. Which date does it count for?
clarifications.a: Monday: its run_date.

clarifications.q: A run succeeded on time and a repair run succeeded an hour after the deadline. Is the date MET?
clarifications.a: No. The repair replaced the output, so the date was final only after the deadline: LATE.

clarifications.q: And if the repair after an on-time success failed?
clarifications.a: A failed run delivers nothing and replaces nothing, so the on-time success stands: MET.

clarifications.q: Is a run that ends exactly at the deadline on time?
clarifications.a: Yes, the deadline is inclusive.

clarifications.q: How is minutes_late rounded?
clarifications.a: Up: 61 seconds late is 2 minutes.

clarifications.q: Which time zone?
clarifications.a: UTC throughout; the session is set to UTC.

hints: Build the report grain first: the dates in the window crossed with the jobs whose schedule is in effect, then attach runs to it.
MAX(end_ts) FILTER (WHERE result_state = 'SUCCESS') and COUNT(*) grouped by job_id, run_date give delivered_at and runs in one pass.
In PostgreSQL, date + time is a timestamp; AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' makes it a timestamptz, and sla_minutes * INTERVAL '1 minute' adds the SLA.
followups: A downstream dashboard should show "SLA met" the moment the first success lands and flip to "restated" if a repair replaces it. What extra columns would you report, and from which rows?
Jobs now run in each team's own time zone, with schedule_time local. What happens to the deadline on daylight-saving days?
The runs table holds five years of history for 40 000 jobs and the report runs every 15 minutes. How would you make it incremental, and which runs can still change an old date's status?
Product wants an SLA percentage per job per month. Should a date with a later repair count as met, late or both, and how do you keep the number from silently changing after it was published?

rules.ask: A run succeeded on time and a repair succeeded two hours later. What does your query report, and what did the consumers actually read at the deadline?
A repair run for Monday starts on Tuesday at 01:00. Which row does your query put it on?
A job was scheduled on a date but never started. Does that date appear in your result at all?
Why does the run type matter here? Show a date where filtering on it changes the status.
The run ended 30 seconds after the deadline. What does your expression return, and why is that the right rounding for a lateness report?

templates.title: Table freshness against upstream tables along the lineage
templates.subtopic: recursive CTEs over a dependency graph, as-of filtering, top-1 per group

sections.scenario: A lakehouse holds bronze (raw), silver (cleaned) and gold (business-level) tables, plus feature tables for models. Every table in the open table format keeps a commit history: one row per version with its timestamp and operation. A catalogue records which table reads which. When a gold table looks stale, the first question is: has anything upstream changed since this table was last refreshed, and how far behind is it?
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that describes every table as of {{as_of}} and returns table_name, last_change, staleness_minutes, ancestors, newer_ancestors, lag_minutes, newest_ancestor, one row per table, ordered by table_name. A table's last_change is the latest commit_ts at or before {{as_of}} among its commits that change data: every operation except OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, which only rewrite or delete files. staleness_minutes is the whole minutes (rounded down) from last_change to {{as_of}}. The lineage table lists direct dependencies (downstream reads upstream); a table's ancestors are everything it depends on directly or indirectly, each counted once. newer_ancestors counts the ancestors whose last_change is strictly later than the table's own. newest_ancestor is the one among those with the latest last_change (ties: the smallest name), or NULL if there is none; lag_minutes is the whole minutes (rounded down) from the table's last_change to that ancestor's, or 0 if there is none. {{view_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The lineage is acyclic. There are {{objects}} objects in catalog_objects.
sections.assumptions: Table names, timestamps and lineage are hypothetical. Treating OPTIMIZE and VACUUM as non-data operations is this exercise's rule (they compact or remove files without changing table contents); check the current docs of your table format for the full list of operations and their data-change flags.
sections.criteria: Data-changing commits only, at or before the as-of time (Hard+); a recursive closure with distinct ancestors (diamonds, Hard+); strictly-newer comparison; the newest ancestor with a deterministic tie-break; minutes rounded down; views traversed but not reported or counted (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss incremental closure, partition-level freshness and lineage history.

clarifications.q: Does an OPTIMIZE after the last write make the table fresher?
clarifications.a: No. It rewrites files with the same data.

clarifications.q: Commits after {{as_of}}?
clarifications.a: Ignore them: the report describes the tables at {{as_of}}.

clarifications.q: A table reaches the same bronze table through two silver tables. How many ancestors is that?
clarifications.a: One.

clarifications.q: Does a table count as newer if it changed at exactly the same second?
clarifications.a: No, newer means strictly later.

clarifications.q: How is a fraction of a minute treated?
clarifications.a: Rounded down, for both staleness and lag.

hints: Compute the transitive closure first: a recursive CTE that starts from lineage and keeps joining lineage on the ancestor it has reached so far.
Use UNION, not UNION ALL, in the recursion so a pair reached by two paths appears once.
Join the closure to the per-table last_change twice (once for the table, once for the ancestor) and aggregate with FILTER; pick the newest ancestor with DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER().
followups: A gold table depends on a slowly changing reference table that is updated monthly. How would you stop it from dominating "newest ancestor" alerts, without hiding real staleness?
The catalogue has 200 000 tables and the lineage graph is deep. How would you compute this every five minutes without recomputing the whole closure?

A table can be correct even when an upstream changed after it (for example, the upstream change is a late partition the table does not read yet). What finer-grained signal would you use instead of table-level timestamps?
The lineage itself changes over time. How would you answer "was this table stale at 09:00 last Tuesday" correctly?

rules.ask: Your recursion uses UNION ALL. What happens to the ancestor counts when a table reaches the same source through two paths?
Why should an OPTIMIZE commit not count as a change? Show a table whose answer changes if it does.
How does your recursive CTE terminate, and what would happen if the lineage had a cycle?
Where in your query does the walk pass through a node with no commits, such as a view?
Which commits are inside that MAX? Name the two filters it needs.

templates.title: Idle minutes on interactive clusters before auto-termination
templates.subtopic: gaps and islands, interval merging with running MAX, LEAD, capped sums

sections.scenario: Teams share interactive (all-purpose) compute clusters for notebooks and ad-hoc jobs. An interactive cluster keeps running, and costing money, between pieces of work until it has been idle for its auto-termination time; job clusters, by contrast, exist only for the run they serve. A FinOps review wants, per owning team, how much interactive cluster time was busy, how much was idle while waiting to auto-terminate, and how often clusters had to be started again.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns owner, clusters, runs, busy_minutes, idle_minutes, starts, idle_share for activity up to {{as_of}}: one row per owner with at least one run on an interactive cluster, ordered by idle_minutes descending, then owner. Only interactive clusters count, and only those with at least one run. Runs on the same cluster can overlap; a cluster is busy whenever at least one run is executing (merge overlapping or touching runs into busy intervals). Between two busy intervals with a gap of g seconds, a cluster with auto-termination T minutes is idle for min(g, T·60) seconds; if g ≥ T·60 it terminated and was started again by the next run. After its last busy interval it is idle for min(T·60, seconds until {{as_of}}). starts is 1 per cluster plus each restart. busy_minutes and idle_minutes are summed per owner and rounded to 2 decimals; idle_share is idle ÷ (idle + busy) per owner, rounded to 4 decimals. {{extra_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{runs}} runs. Cluster start-up time and pricing are out of scope.
sections.assumptions: Teams, clusters and times are hypothetical. Terminating after exactly T idle minutes, and treating a run that starts at that instant as a new start, is this exercise's simplified model; real auto-termination also depends on what counts as activity (check current docs).
sections.criteria: Interactive clusters only, and only with runs; busy time as merged intervals (Hard+); gaps measured from the latest end so far, not the previous row (Hard+); idle capped at the auto-termination time with an inclusive restart rule; the trailing idle up to the as-of time; disabled auto-termination and still-running runs (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss choosing a termination time and detecting fake activity.

clarifications.q: Two notebooks run on the same cluster at the same time. Is that double the busy time?
clarifications.a: No. Busy time is the union of the run intervals.

clarifications.q: One run ends at 10:00:00 and the next starts at 10:00:00. Is there a gap?
clarifications.a: No: they form one busy interval.

clarifications.q: A gap of exactly T minutes?
clarifications.a: The cluster was idle for T minutes, had just terminated, and was started again: one restart.

clarifications.q: Does an interactive cluster that never ran count?
clarifications.a: No. Only clusters with at least one run.

clarifications.q: What about job clusters?
clarifications.a: Exclude them; they are not idle between runs.

hints: Order each cluster's runs by start_ts and compute the latest end_ts among all earlier runs with MAX(end_ts) OVER (… ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING). A run that starts after it begins a new busy interval.
A running SUM of that "starts a new interval" flag numbers the islands; group by it to get each busy interval's start and end.
LEAD(start) over the islands gives each gap; the last island's gap runs to {{as_of}}. Cap with LEAST.
followups: Recommend an auto-termination time per team from this data. What would you compute, and what does a shorter time cost the people using the cluster?
A cluster takes about five minutes to start. How would you account for start-up time in "idle" and in the recommendation?
This must run daily across every workspace with billions of run events. How would you partition the work so that a busy interval crossing midnight is still measured correctly?
Some interactive clusters keep a notebook attached that polls every minute, so they never look idle. How would you detect clusters that are "busy" but doing no useful work?

rules.ask: A long run contains a short one, and the next run starts after the short one ends but before the long one ends. What gap does your query compute?
Two runs overlap for half an hour. How much busy time does your query report for that half hour?
Which comparison decides a restart, and what happens at a gap of exactly T minutes?
Why are job clusters excluded? What would including them do to idle_share?
What starts a new island in your query: the previous run's end, or the latest end so far? Show a case where they differ.

templates.title: Stage DAG — critical path and makespan on a fixed number of slots
templates.subtopic: topological sort, longest path in a DAG, heaps, discrete-event simulation

sections.scenario: A distributed query engine such as Apache Spark splits a job into stages connected by shuffles: a stage can start only when every stage it reads from has finished. A capacity planner for a lakehouse platform wants two numbers for a job before buying more executors: the critical path (the fastest the job could ever finish, with unlimited slots) and the makespan it actually gets on slots executor slots under a simple priority rule.
sections.problem: Implement schedule(stages, slots). Each stage is (stage_id, tasks, task_seconds, deps): deps lists the stage ids it depends on. {{task_rule}} A stage's bottom level is its task_seconds plus the largest bottom level among the stages that depend on it (0 if none). Return (critical_path_seconds, critical_path, makespan): critical_path_seconds is the largest bottom level; critical_path is the list of stage ids found by starting at the stage with the largest bottom level and repeatedly moving to the dependent stage with the largest bottom level, until a stage has no dependents (ties at every step: the smaller stage_id). makespan comes from simulating, from time 0: whenever slots are free, give them to the ready stage with the largest bottom level (ties: the smaller stage_id), starting as many of its remaining tasks as there are free slots, and continue with the next ready stage while slots remain. A stage is ready once all its dependencies have finished; tasks that finish at time t free their slots, and make their dependents ready, before anything starts at t. Started tasks run to completion. makespan is the time the last task finishes. {{invalid_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 30 000 stages and 120 000 dependencies; 1 ≤ task_seconds ≤ 10⁴; 1 ≤ slots ≤ 1 000; stage ids are unique integers. The list is in no particular order. O((n + E) log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Durations are hypothetical and fixed; a real scheduler has speculative execution, locality, retries and variable task times, none of which are modelled here.
sections.criteria: Correct bottom levels and a deterministic critical path; finish-before-start ordering at equal times; a fixed priority with id tie-break; slots given to the next ready stage when the top one needs fewer; invalid input returns None (Hard+); multi-task stages occupy several slots and finish with their last task (Very Hard); O((n + E) log n) with heaps; can reason about lower bounds, skew and slot counts.

clarifications.q: Does the critical path depend on slots?
clarifications.a: No. It assumes unlimited slots: each stage takes task_seconds.

clarifications.q: A dependency finishes at t = 10 and a slot is free. Can the dependent start at t = 10?
clarifications.a: Yes. Finishes at a time are processed before starts at that time.

clarifications.q: Is the priority fixed, or does it change during the run?
clarifications.a: Fixed: each stage's bottom level, computed once.

clarifications.q: The highest-priority ready stage needs fewer slots than are free. What happens to the rest?
clarifications.a: They go to the next ready stage by priority, at the same instant.

clarifications.q: Is the list order meaningful?
clarifications.a: No. It is not a topological order.

hints: Build the dependents lists and in-degrees; Kahn's algorithm gives a topological order and detects a cycle at the same time (fewer stages come out than went in).
Bottom levels: walk the topological order backwards.
For the simulation keep two heaps: ready stages keyed by (-bottom_level, stage_id), and running batches keyed by finish time. Jump from one finish time to the next; never step second by second.
followups: Prove that the makespan is never below the critical path, and never below the total task-seconds divided by slots. When does list scheduling come close to the larger of the two?
One stage's tasks are skewed: one task takes 20× the median. How does that change both numbers, and what would you change in the model?
The planner asks: "how many slots until more stop helping?" How would you answer from this function without trying every value?
Stages now have a memory requirement and each slot has a memory limit, so some stages need two slots per task. How does the priority rule change, and what can go wrong?

rules.ask: The longest dependency chain is 20 000 stages. What happens to your recursive version in CPython, and how would you make it iterative?
Why is the priority the bottom level rather than the stage's own length? Give a three-stage example where they disagree.
Task times go up to 10 000 seconds. How many iterations does a per-second loop make, and how do you jump between events instead?
How many times does your loop look at each stage over the whole run? What does that cost with 30 000 stages?
How does your topological sort tell you there was a cycle, and what do you return then?

templates.title: Table snapshots from a transaction log with checkpoints
templates.subtopic: log replay, binary search, offline query batching

sections.scenario: An open table format stores a table as data files plus a transaction log: each version is a commit listing files added and removed, and every so often a checkpoint records the complete list of active files so readers do not have to replay the whole log. Time travel ("read the table as of version 1 742") rebuilds the file list at that version. A storage audit wants the number of files and bytes for thousands of historical versions at once.
sections.problem: Implement snapshot_sizes(commits, checkpoints, versions). commits maps a version to its list of actions, each ("add", path, size) or ("remove", path). checkpoints maps a version to the full list of (path, size) active after that version. To rebuild version v: start from the checkpoint with the largest version c ≤ v (or from an empty table before version 0 if there is none), then apply commits c+1, …, v in order, each commit's actions in list order. An add makes the path active with that size (replacing the size if it was already active); a remove makes it inactive (a remove of a path that is not active does nothing). For each entry of versions, return (file_count, total_bytes) of the rebuilt version, in the same order. The latest version is the largest version that has a commit or a checkpoint. {{log_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 3 000 versions, 30 000 queries, and checkpoints of up to 10 000 files; queries can repeat and come in any order. Rebuilding every query from scratch is too slow: aim for each commit to be replayed about once.
sections.assumptions: Paths, sizes and the checkpoint interval are hypothetical. This is a simplified model of a table-format log (no metadata, protocol or deletion-vector actions, single-file checkpoints); check the format's current specification for the real reconciliation rules.
sections.criteria: Correct base checkpoint (after-commit semantics); actions in order with replace and ignore rules; empty table versus None; None for out-of-range and unrebuildable versions without raising (Hard+); a missing commit poisoning only the versions that need it (Very Hard); one replay per checkpoint group with a running total; can discuss checkpoint discovery, commit conflicts and retention.

clarifications.q: Is a checkpoint at version c the state before or after commit c?
clarifications.a: After: it already includes commit c.

clarifications.q: If the commit file for a checkpoint's own version is missing, can I still read that version?
clarifications.a: Yes. The checkpoint is enough; commit c is never replayed when starting from checkpoint c.

clarifications.q: A table whose files were all removed?
clarifications.a: It exists: (0, 0), not None.

clarifications.q: Can I trust a checkpoint over replaying the log from an older checkpoint?
clarifications.a: Always start from the latest checkpoint at or below the version, as specified.

clarifications.q: Should I raise on a version I cannot rebuild?
clarifications.a: No. Return None for it and carry on.

hints: Sort the checkpoint versions once; bisect_right finds the base checkpoint for any version in O(log K).
Group the queries by base checkpoint and sort each group by version: one forward replay per group answers every query in it.
Keep a running total_bytes as you apply actions, adjusting by the old size on a re-add, so a query never sums the whole file list.
followups: Readers usually want the latest version. How does a reader find the newest checkpoint without listing the whole log directory, and what happens if that pointer is stale?
Two writers commit version 1 801 at the same moment. How does the log make exactly one of them win, and what must the loser do before retrying?
Checkpoints of a table with ten million files are huge. How would you make them cheaper to write and to read for a query that needs one partition?
Old log files are cleaned up after a retention period. What does that do to time travel, and how would you report which versions are still readable?

rules.ask: Commits below version 400 were cleaned up. What does your code return for version 1 000, and is that right?
Which bisect gives the checkpoint at or below v, and what happens when v is exactly a checkpoint version?
How many times does your code add up the file sizes over 30 000 queries, and how would you avoid it?
How many times do you copy a checkpoint's file list? Could you copy it once per checkpoint instead of once per query?
Two writers both read version 1 800 and both try to write 1 801. What exactly makes one fail, and what does it check before retrying?

templates.title: Salting hot join keys and balancing the tasks
templates.subtopic: skewed joins, salting, largest-first placement with a heap

sections.scenario: A nightly Spark job joins a large table of events with a smaller table on {{key_name}}. A shuffle sends every row of one key to one task, so a handful of very large keys keep a few tasks running for hours while the rest finish in minutes. A common remedy is salting: split a hot key's rows into several pieces with an extra salt column, copy the matching rows from the other side of the join to every salt, and join on the key and the salt together. Before the job starts, a planner reads row counts per key from table statistics, decides how many salts each key gets, and decides which task processes each piece.
sections.problem:
Implement plan_tasks(key_rows, num_tasks, target_rows, max_salts=None, other_rows=None). key_rows maps each key to its number of rows on the large side, always at least 1.

  1. Salts. A key with r rows gets s = 1 piece when r <= target_rows, and s = ceil(r / target_rows) pieces when r > target_rows. {{salt_rule}}
  2. Shares. The rows are split as evenly as possible. Salt i, counting from 0, gets r // s rows, plus one more row if i < r % s.
  3. Load. A piece's load is its share of rows. {{other_rule}}
  4. Placement. Take the pieces in order of load, largest first. Break ties by key, then by salt, both ascending. Put each piece on the task whose current load is smallest, and break a tie between tasks by the lowest task index.
  5. Result. Return (largest_load, tasks). tasks is a list of num_tasks lists, and list t holds the (key, salt) tuples placed on task t, in the order they were placed. A key that is not split appears as (key, 0). With no keys, every task is empty and largest_load is 0.
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 keys and 5 000 tasks. Row counts are integers below 10⁹, and target_rows is at least 1. The pieces must be placed in close to O(P log P) time for P pieces. Scanning every task for every piece is too slow at this size.
sections.assumptions: Row counts and sizes are hypothetical, and the statistics are taken as exact. A task's run time is proportional to its load, and all executors are identical. The salt itself is assigned to rows later, by the job, so only the counts matter here.
sections.criteria: Correct number of salts at the boundary (r == target_rows is not split); remainder rows given to the lowest salts; max_salts applied after the ceiling; other-side rows added to every piece without changing s; one sort with the full tie rule; least-loaded placement with the lowest-index tie, using a heap; empty tasks kept in the result; integer arithmetic; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on stale statistics, adaptive execution and broadcast joins.

clarifications.q: Does the other side of the join change the number of salts?
clarifications.a: No. Only the large side's row count decides s. The other side only adds to the load of each piece.

clarifications.q: Is a key with exactly target_rows rows split?
clarifications.a: No. It is split only when it has more rows than target_rows.

clarifications.q: Is this the best possible schedule?
clarifications.a: No. Largest first onto the least-loaded task is a greedy rule with a known worst case of 4/3 − 1/(3m) times the optimal makespan on m tasks. You must follow the rule exactly so that the answer is unique.

clarifications.q: Does the order of keys in the dict matter?
clarifications.a: No. The answer must not depend on it, which is why the tie rules exist.

clarifications.q: Can there be more tasks than pieces?
clarifications.a: Yes. The remaining tasks stay empty, as empty lists.

hints: Build every piece first, then sort once with a key that encodes all the tie rules: load descending, then key, then salt.
"The least-loaded task, lowest index on a tie" is the minimum of (load, index) pairs. A heap of those pairs gives it in O(log T).
With other_rows, a key split into s pieces carries its other-side rows s times. Add them to each piece's load before you sort.
followups: The row counts come from statistics that can be 30% out of date. How would you make the plan robust, and what would you measure during the run to know it worked?
Spark's adaptive query execution can split skewed shuffle partitions at run time. When is a planner like this still worth having, and when would you leave skew to the engine?

For one hot key the other side is large too, so copying it to every salt is expensive. How would you choose the number of salts to minimise the largest task, and when would you broadcast the other side instead?
Half the executors are slower spot instances. How does the placement rule change, and what happens to the 4/3 guarantee?

rules.ask: How many operations does finding the least-loaded task take for 200 000 pieces on 5 000 tasks, and how would you bring that down?
What exactly is in each heap entry, and how does the entry make a tie between two tasks go to the lower index?
A random salt makes the split differ every time the task runs. What happens when a failed task is retried, and how would a deterministic salt avoid that?
Round-robin placement ignores loads. Build a small case where it makes the largest task twice as large as the greedy plan does.
Broadcasting the smaller side avoids the shuffle and the salting. What size decides it, and what fails when that side grows past it?
Does math.ceil(r / target_rows) stay exact for every integer row count? Write the integer-only form.

templates.title: Small-file compaction plan for a partitioned table
templates.subtopic: first-fit decreasing with a segment tree, table maintenance

sections.scenario: Streaming writers and frequent small appends leave a lakehouse table, partitioned by {{partition_col}}, with thousands of small files in each partition. Every query opens each file, so reads slow down and the table's metadata grows. A maintenance job rewrites the small files into larger ones of about {{target_mb}} MB, much as an OPTIMIZE-style compaction does. Before it runs, a planner decides which files are combined into which output file, partition by partition, so that the job is predictable and its plan can be reviewed. In the samples, a file is small when it is under {{small_mb}} MB.
sections.problem:
Implement plan_compaction(files, target_mb, small_mb, min_input_files=2, purge_pct=None). files is a list of (path, partition, size_mb, deleted_mb), where deleted_mb is the size of rows that are marked deleted but still stored in the file (0 <= deleted_mb < size_mb).

  1. Candidates. A file is a candidate if size_mb < small_mb. {{purge_rule}} A candidate weighs its live size, size_mb - deleted_mb, because only live rows are written out.
  2. Partitions. Each partition is planned on its own, and an output file never mixes partitions. {{partition_rule}}
  3. Packing. Within a partition, take the candidates by weight, largest first, and break ties by path, ascending. Put each one into the earliest-opened output whose total weight plus this file's weight is at most target_mb. If there is none, open a new output. This is first-fit decreasing.
  4. Lone files. An output that ends up with a single file is dropped from the plan, because rewriting one small file gains nothing. It is kept if that file is a purge candidate, because the rewrite removes its deleted rows.
  5. Result. Return a list of (partition, output_mb, paths), where output_mb is the output's total weight and paths lists its files in the order they were placed. Order the list by partition, ascending, then by the order in which outputs were opened. Return [] when there is nothing to do.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 files per table, and up to 100 000 in one partition. Sizes are integer MB below 2 * target_mb, small_mb <= target_mb, and every candidate's weight is at most target_mb. Close to O(n log n) is expected. A partition can have tens of thousands of outputs, so scanning the open outputs for every file is too slow.
sections.assumptions: File sizes, thresholds and counts are hypothetical. An output's size is the sum of its inputs' live sizes; compression and file footers are ignored. The job replaces each output's inputs atomically, so readers see either the old files or the new one.
sections.criteria: Candidate rule with a strict < small_mb boundary; live size as the weight; partitions planned independently and listed in order; first fit, not best fit, with ties by path; the at-most boundary on target_mb; lone outputs dropped unless they purge deleted rows; min_input_files applied to all candidates; a segment tree (or another structure) that keeps first-fit order in O(log n); a clear complexity argument; credible answers on concurrent writers, clustering, resumption and a rewrite budget.

clarifications.q: Is first-fit decreasing the best packing?
clarifications.a: No. Optimal bin packing is NP-hard. First-fit decreasing never uses more than 11/9 of the optimal number of outputs plus a small constant, which is good enough for maintenance. You must follow it exactly so that the plan is unique.

clarifications.q: May an output be exactly target_mb?
clarifications.a: Yes. The limit is "at most".

clarifications.q: Can two partitions share an output file?
clarifications.a: No. An output file belongs to exactly one partition.

clarifications.q: What if every candidate in a partition ends up alone?
clarifications.a: Then that partition contributes nothing to the plan.

clarifications.q: A small file has some deleted rows. Does it count at its full size?
clarifications.a: No. Every candidate weighs its live size.

hints: Group the candidates by partition and sort each group once by (-weight, path).
You need the leftmost output whose free space is at least w. A max segment tree over the outputs' free space finds it in O(log n): go left whenever the left child has enough room.
Give outputs that are not opened yet full room in the tree. The leftmost of them is exactly the next output to open, so "no output fits" needs no special case.
followups: Streaming writers keep appending to the newest partition while compaction runs. How do you avoid conflicting with them, and which partitions would you leave out?
Readers would also gain from rows clustered by a frequently filtered column. How would the plan change if outputs were also sorted by that column, and what does it cost?
The job fails halfway through a partition. What does the table look like, and how do you resume without rewriting the outputs that already committed?
The nightly budget allows rewriting 2 TB, and there are 20 TB of candidates. Which outputs would you choose first, and how would you measure the benefit afterwards?

rules.ask: Best fit is a valid heuristic, but this plan is first fit. Where do the two differ for files of 74, 58, 56 and 13 MB with a target of 128 MB?
A sorted list of free space finds the tightest output, not the earliest one. How would you keep first-fit order with that structure?
How do you find the leftmost output with enough room, and what do outputs that are not opened yet hold in your tree?
How many outputs can one partition reach here, and what does a scan cost over the whole partition?
A writer appends to the partition while your rewrite runs. What does the table's commit protocol check, and which of the two commits fails?

templates.title: Debug the upsert (MERGE) into a customers table
templates.subtopic: MERGE semantics, source deduplication, null keys, stale changes

sections.scenario: A customers table in a lakehouse is kept current from the billing system's change feed. Each micro-batch of changes is merged into the table: new customers are inserted, plan changes update the row and closed accounts are deleted. A SQL MERGE fails when several source rows match one target row, and SQL never matches a NULL key, so the pipeline deduplicates and filters each batch in code before applying it. The support team has raised five complaints. Customer 0, the oldest account, never changes and is reported as a null key. When two plan changes for one customer carry the same timestamp, the table sometimes keeps the earlier one. Rows with an empty plan appear for customers who were never in the table. A customer who upgraded was then deleted by an older close event that was replayed. And the weekly backfill merge has started to run for hours. The code below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix merge_upsert(target, changes) so that it meets this specification. target is a list of rows {"id", "plan", "updated_at"} with unique ids, none of them None. changes is a list of {"id", "op", "plan", "updated_at", "seq"}, where op is "upsert" or "delete", plan is None for a delete, and seq is the change's position in the feed (unique, larger means later). {{batch_rule}}

  1. Null keys. A change whose id is None is never matched or applied. It is counted in null_keys. Every other id, including 0, is a real key.
  2. One change per key. For each key, only the change with the greatest (updated_at, seq) counts. The other changes for that key are ignored and not counted anywhere.
  3. Stale changes. If the key is in the table and the change's updated_at is earlier than the row's, the change is stale: it is counted in stale and nothing changes. This applies to deletes as well as upserts. An equal updated_at is not stale.
  4. Apply. An upsert of an existing key sets plan and updated_at from the change (updated). An upsert of a missing key inserts the row (inserted). A delete of an existing key removes the row (deleted). A delete of a missing key does nothing and is not counted.
  5. Output. {"rows": [[id, plan, updated_at], ...], "inserted", "updated", "deleted", "stale", "null_keys"}, with rows sorted by id.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Up to 100 000 rows and 100 000 changes per batch, processed in O((n + m) log(n + m)) time or better.
sections.assumptions: The table, plans, ids and timestamps are hypothetical and simplified. updated_at is an integer timestamp from the billing system. Changes may arrive in any order within a batch, because files are read in parallel.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom; is None for null keys, so 0 is a real key; deduplication by (updated_at, seq); the stale check before both update and delete; no insert for a delete of a missing key; a hash index instead of a list scan and list.remove; minimal fixes that keep the output format; a test per bug; sound answers on replays, tombstones, SQL MERGE and history.

clarifications.q: Is customer 0 a real customer?
clarifications.a: Yes. Only None is a null key.

clarifications.q: Two changes for one key have the same updated_at. Which wins?
clarifications.a: The one with the larger seq, which was written to the feed later.

clarifications.q: Does a delete need a timestamp check too?
clarifications.a: Yes. An older delete must not remove a newer row.

clarifications.q: What happens to a delete for a customer the table does not have?
clarifications.a: Nothing. It is not an insert and it is not counted.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds, including one that only shows on a large batch. The checks point at each one.

hints: Read the null-key test aloud for the value 0.
Write down two changes for one key with the same updated_at and seq 4 then 7. Which one does the code keep?
Walk a delete through the code for a key that is not in the table, and then for a key whose row is newer than the delete.
Count how many rows the code looks at to find one match, and how many it moves when it removes one.
followups: After a restart the same batch is merged twice. Is the result the same? Which counters change on the second run, and does anyone depend on them?
A delete arrives in an earlier batch than the insert it cancels. Under rule 4 the delete is lost and the insert wins. How would you keep tombstones, and for how long?
Write the same logic as one SQL MERGE: the deduplication, the matched clauses with their conditions, and the not-matched clause. Where do the null keys go?
Finance now wants every plan a customer has had, with dates (slowly changing dimension type 2). What changes in the merge?

rules.ask: Where else in a pipeline does a truthiness test drop a valid value such as 0, an empty string or False?
Your deduplication orders by updated_at. What makes the order total when two changes share it?
Your index holds the whole table in memory. At 500 million rows, where would the merge run instead, and how would the engine find matching rows?
How long do you keep a tombstone, and what happens to an insert that arrives after its tombstone has expired?
Merging the same batch twice leaves the same rows. Do the counters match too, and who reads them?

templates.title: Incremental file ingestion with schema evolution and a rescued-data column
templates.subtopic: incremental file discovery, exactly-once loading, schema evolution

sections.scenario: Partner systems drop files into cloud object storage: about {{files_per_day}} new files a day from {{sources}} sources, as {{file_format}}. A bronze table on the lakehouse must receive every record of every file exactly once, within {{freshness}} of the file landing. Sources add fields without notice, change a field's type (an id that was a number arrives as a string), change the case of a field name, and send malformed records. Some lakehouse ingestion tools discover new files incrementally, infer and evolve a schema, and keep values that do not fit the schema in a rescued-data column instead of dropping them. This exercise assumes such a column; check current docs for any specific product's behaviour.
sections.problem: Design the ingestion from object storage to the bronze table. Cover how new files are discovered (directory listing or storage event notifications) and how the pipeline remembers which files it has processed; how each file's records reach the table exactly once, including after a crash; the schema policy (new columns, type changes, case differences, nested fields) and who approves a change; what goes into the rescued-data column and how it is used; malformed records; reprocessing one source's history; small files; and what you monitor.
sections.constraints: No file may be skipped or loaded twice. A new field from one source must not stop ingestion for the other sources for more than a few minutes. No value may be silently dropped. Reprocessing one source's last 30 days must not duplicate records. A source occasionally overwrites a file at the same path with corrected content. Some files arrive days late, with old dates in their paths.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, source counts and latencies are hypothetical. Files are immutable once written, except for the overwrites described above. Each record carries a source id; most carry an event time. You may use common building blocks: object storage notifications and queues, a stream processor with checkpoints, and a table format with atomic commits.
sections.criteria: Incremental discovery with a durable record of processed files and a reconciliation listing for gaps; exactly-once loading through a checkpoint and an atomic table commit; file identity that tells an overwrite from a replay, with replacement of the earlier load; an explicit schema policy per kind of change with an approval path; a rescued-data column that keeps every unfit value with its source context; counted, never silent, handling of malformed records; isolation so one source cannot stall the others; reprocessing without duplicates; monitoring of lag, rescued volume and schema changes; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is listing the bucket good enough?
clarifications.a: At {{files_per_day}} files a day, listing a large prefix gets slower every day. You decide, and you explain what you use for backfills and for gaps.

clarifications.q: What does "exactly once" mean when a file is overwritten?
clarifications.a: The corrected content must replace the earlier load of that file, not add to it.

clarifications.q: Can a field's type change permanently?
clarifications.a: Yes. Some changes are mistakes that will be reverted, and some are deliberate. The pipeline cannot tell which on its own.

clarifications.q: Who reads the bronze table?
clarifications.a: Silver pipelines, which need a stable schema, and engineers investigating a source, who need every original value.

clarifications.q: Is the rescued-data column one column per table?
clarifications.a: Yes, a single semi-structured column holding the fields and values that did not fit, with enough context to trace them back to the file.

hints: Separate discovery from loading. Whatever discovers files must hand the loader a durable list that it can replay after a crash.
Record a file's identity as more than its path: path plus size, modification time or an etag tells an overwrite from a replay.
Decide per kind of change: a new column can be added automatically, a type change goes to the rescued-data column until someone decides, and a case difference is a rule you state once.
followups: A source changes amount from a number to a string for two days, then back. Walk through what the bronze table holds, what silver sees, and how you repair it afterwards.
The storage notification service drops events for an hour. How do you find and load the files you never heard about?
A source re-sends 30 days of corrected files under the same paths. How do you replace the old records without duplicating them, and what do downstream tables see?
One source sends a 40 GB file while the others send 5 MB files. What happens to {{freshness}} for everyone else, and what would you change?
A compliance request requires removing one customer's records from bronze. Where are they, including inside the rescued-data column?

rules.ask: How long does listing take when the prefix holds a year of files, and how do you avoid listing it all on every run?
Notifications can be delayed, duplicated or lost. What do you do with each, and what reconciles the gaps?
Automatic evolution adds a column the moment a source sends it. What happens when a source sends a typo for an existing field?
Who looks at the rescued-data column, how often, and what turns a value in it back into a proper column?
Which records would you lose, and how would you know how many?

incidents: One of the {{sources}} sources renames customer_id to customerId on a Friday evening; by Monday a third of its records have a null customer_id in silver and the new field sits in the rescued-data column.

The storage notifications are delayed by 90 minutes during a cloud provider incident, so the {{freshness}} target is missed for every source at once, and then a burst of a quarter of a day's files arrives together.
A source overwrites 2 000 files with corrected content; the next morning the silver totals for those days are exactly double.

templates.title: Streaming aggregation with watermarks and bounded state
templates.subtopic: event time, watermarks, state size, late data, restarts

window: session windows that close after 30 minutes of inactivity

sections.scenario: A product-telemetry stream carries about {{events_per_sec}} events a second from client applications. A dashboard and an alerting job need counts and distinct users per key, over {{window}}, for {{keys}}. Mobile and desktop clients buffer events while offline, so events can arrive up to {{lateness}} after they happened, and occasionally later. The aggregation runs on a stream processor with checkpointed state, such as Spark Structured Streaming, and writes its results to a lakehouse table.
sections.problem: Design the streaming aggregation. Cover event time against processing time; the watermark you choose and what it does to latency, completeness and state size; when a window's result is emitted and whether it can change afterwards; what happens to events that arrive after the watermark; how big the state gets and how you bound it; exact or approximate distinct counts; restarts, checkpoints and changes to the query; an exactly-once write to the results table; skew from very large keys; and how a backfill fits with the live stream.
sections.constraints: The dashboard needs a first result within a few minutes of a window closing. Alerts must not fire twice for the same window. State must fit the cluster's memory and disk with headroom, and checkpoints must finish well within the trigger interval. Finance-grade daily totals are produced by a separate batch job, but they must agree with the stream within a documented tolerance.
sections.assumptions: All rates, key counts and lateness figures are hypothetical. Each event has an event id, a key, a user id and an event time set by the client. Client clocks can be wrong. The input is a partitioned log that keeps seven days of data.
sections.criteria: Event-time windows with a watermark whose delay is justified against {{lateness}} and sized in state; a clear emission policy per consumer (final for alerts, corrected early results for the dashboard); late events beyond the watermark kept in a side table and reconciled by batch; bounded state through watermarks, deduplication windows and state TTL; approximate distinct counts with mergeable sketches where the target allows; an idempotent sink keyed by batch; a plan for query changes that cannot reuse the checkpoint; skew handling for very large keys; guards against clock skew; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: How does the watermark move?
clarifications.a: Assume the common rule: the largest event time seen so far, minus the delay you configure. State for windows that end before the watermark can be dropped.

clarifications.q: Can a result change after it was shown?
clarifications.a: You decide, and the dashboard and the alerting job may need different answers.

clarifications.q: Are events ever duplicated?
clarifications.a: Yes. Clients retry, so the same event id can arrive twice, minutes apart.

clarifications.q: Do distinct users have to be exact?
clarifications.a: On the dashboard, within 2%. In the daily batch totals, exact.

clarifications.q: What happens to an event older than {{lateness}}?
clarifications.a: It must not change the stream's results, but it must not disappear either.

hints: A longer watermark delay buys completeness with latency and state. Write the state size as keys × open windows × bytes per window before you choose it.
Separate the two consumers: alerts want one final answer per window, and the dashboard can take early results that are corrected later.
Make the sink idempotent: a batch that is written twice after a restart must leave the table unchanged.
followups: A client release ships with its clock a year in the future. What does that do to your watermark and to every on-time event after it, and how do you guard against it?
You must add a new grouping column to the aggregation. Can the job restart from its checkpoint, and if not, how do you switch over without a gap or double counting?
State grows by 5% a day and checkpoints now take longer than the trigger interval. Where does the state come from, and what do you change?
One key produces 30% of all events. What happens to the task that owns it, and what would you change?
The daily batch total and the stream disagree by 4% for one day. How do you find out whether the stream or the batch is wrong?

rules.ask: A client comes back online after six hours and sends its buffer. Which window do those events land in with your choice, and what does the dashboard show?
Complete mode rewrites the whole result every trigger. How big is that result for {{keys}}, and how long does each trigger take?
Can two windows' sketches be merged into a daily figure, and what error does the 2% target allow?
How long must you remember an event id to catch a retry, and what does that add to the state?
After a crash the same micro-batch is written again. What key makes the second write a no-op?

incidents: A client build with a clock set a year ahead sends a few hundred events; the maximum event time jumps, the watermark moves past every open window, and every on-time event after that is treated as late.
After a deploy adds a grouping column, the job refuses to restart from its checkpoint; the dashboard has had no data for 40 minutes and the input log keeps only seven days.
At {{events_per_sec}} events a second with {{lateness}} of allowed lateness, state reaches the cluster's disk limit during a holiday traffic peak.

templates.title: Clickstream in bronze, silver and gold — schema drift and a quarantine that gets read
templates.subtopic: medallion layers, event grain, schema evolution, rescued data, quarantine, replay-safe deduplication

sections.scenario: A retailer runs its analytics on a lakehouse. Its web site and two mobile apps send clickstream events (page views, searches, add-to-cart, checkout steps) as JSON files that land in cloud object storage, about {{daily_events}} events a day. At any time about {{app_versions}} app versions are live, each with its own idea of the event payload: fields get added, renamed or change type between releases, and old versions keep sending the old shape for months. Phones buffer events offline and upload them up to {{late_days}} days late, and a client retry can upload the same event twice. About {{invalid_share}} of events are unusable as sent (no event time, unknown event type, a user id in the wrong format). The data team wants three layers: a raw layer that never loses anything, a cleaned layer that analysts and data scientists can trust, and business tables (sessions, a daily product funnel, marketing attribution inputs) that the dashboards read.
sections.problem: Design the tables in the three layers (bronze, silver, gold) and the rules between them. Cover: the bronze table's columns and partitioning, including what you keep about where each row came from; how schema changes are handled at each layer (new fields, type changes, renamed fields, fields you did not expect), including a rescued-data column for values that do not fit the declared schema; the silver event table's grain, keys, types and deduplication rule; the quarantine design for unusable events (what is kept, the reason codes, who reads it and how a fixed event re-enters silver); the gold tables' grains; and how late events and replays of bronze flow through to gold without double counting.
sections.constraints: Bronze is append-only and keeps every byte that arrived, including events that fail validation. Silver holds each event once, with typed columns and an event time in UTC. No event disappears silently between bronze and silver: every bronze row is either in silver, in quarantine, or explained by a deduplication rule. Gold numbers for a day can change only while that day is inside the late-arrival window, unless a documented restatement says otherwise.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, version counts and shares are hypothetical. Each event carries a client-generated event id, an app version and a client timestamp; the server adds a receive time. In this exercise the ingestion tool can add new columns to bronze automatically and put values that do not match the declared type into a rescued-data column; check current docs for the exact behaviour.
sections.criteria: Bronze as append-only provenance with the raw or rescued payload; explicit schema-evolution rules per layer (additive changes, type changes into rescued data, renames as deliberate mappings); a silver event grain with a stated deduplication key and window and idempotent writes; quarantine as a queryable table with reason codes, an owner, alerting on its rate and a re-entry path; gold grains with late-data windows and a close; partitions recomputed only where late or replayed data landed; each incident detected, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the client event id unique?
clarifications.a: It is meant to be, per device. A retry resends the same id; a buggy app version once reused ids after reinstall, so you should say what the deduplication key is and why.

clarifications.q: Which time do analysts use, client or server?
clarifications.a: Event time is the client timestamp, but clocks on phones can be wrong by hours. Say how you keep both and when you trust which.

clarifications.q: Who owns the quarantine?
clarifications.a: Today nobody. Part of the answer is who looks at it, how often and what they do with it.

clarifications.q: Can a field change meaning without changing name?
clarifications.a: Yes. One release started sending price in minor units instead of major units. Say how you would notice.

clarifications.q: Must gold tables be rebuilt from scratch when a schema changes?
clarifications.a: No; full rebuilds of {{daily_events}} a day are expensive. Say what is incremental and what is recomputed.

hints: Bronze is about provenance (file, offset or row number, ingest time, app version, the raw payload or rescued data), not about meaning; silver is about meaning.
Decide the deduplication key and window for silver, and make the silver write idempotent so a replay of bronze changes nothing.
Quarantine is a table with a reason code and the raw record, plus a way back into silver; a counter of dropped rows is not a quarantine.
followups: Write the silver deduplication rule. A retried event arrives twice, two days apart, with different receive times. Which copy wins, and what does a replay of last week's bronze files do?
App version 7.3 starts sending duration as a string. What happens in bronze, in silver and in the gold session table that same hour?
Events arrive up to {{late_days}} days late. Which gold partitions does each run touch, and when is a day's funnel final?
A fix for the user-id format means a week of quarantined events are now valid. Walk through how they re-enter silver and gold without counting anything twice.

At {{daily_events}} events a day, how do you lay out bronze and silver (partitioning, clustering, file sizes) so that both the incremental pipeline and an analyst's query for one user's session stay cheap?

rules.ask: About {{invalid_share}} of events are unusable. A product manager asks next month how many checkouts you lost when one app version broke. Where is that answer in your design?
Overwriting a day of silver means re-reading {{daily_events}} events. Which part of your pipeline really needs a recompute, and how do you limit it to the affected days?
Automatic schema evolution added a column called userId next to user_id. What does silver do, and who decides?
What exactly is your key, and over what time window do you deduplicate? What does that window cost in state or in reads?
How many distinct users a day, and how many files does that produce? What would you partition by instead, and how do you still find one user's events quickly?

incidents: A new app release sends the event timestamp in local time without an offset. For two days silver puts about a fifth of mobile events in the wrong hour, and the gold funnel shows a midnight spike; events from those days keep arriving for {{late_days}} days.

The quarantine table grows from {{invalid_share}} to 12% of events after a release renames event_type to type. Nobody is alerted, and the daily checkout funnel drops by a tenth for three days before a marketer asks why.

A storage-notification backlog is replayed and a week of bronze files is ingested a second time. Silver deduplicates, but a gold session table built by appending each run's new silver rows double counts sessions for that week.

templates.title: Slowly changing account dimension with MERGE — late corrections and early facts
templates.subtopic: SCD type 2 with MERGE, back-dated changes, early-arriving facts, surrogate versus business keys

sections.scenario: A software company sells a usage-billed cloud product and analyses usage on a lakehouse. Usage arrives every hour as one row per account, workspace, product and hour, about {{usage_rows}} rows a day. Finance and sales report usage by the account's attributes: pricing tier, sales segment, region, account owner and parent company. Those attributes change for about {{daily_changes}} of {{accounts}} accounts a day and come from a CRM extract delivered daily. The extract is messy: it sends full snapshots of changed accounts, sometimes the same account twice in one file with different values, and corrections that are back-dated up to {{backdate_days}} days ("this account moved to the enterprise tier on the 3rd, not today"). Usage for a brand-new account often arrives before the CRM knows the account exists.
sections.problem: Design the account dimension as a slowly changing dimension (type 2) and the process that maintains it with MERGE statements on the lakehouse. Cover: the columns (business key, surrogate key, validity interval, current flag, a hash of tracked attributes, provenance), which attributes are tracked as history and which are overwritten; the MERGE logic for an ordinary change, including how one MERGE both closes the old version and inserts the new one; how a back-dated change is inserted between existing versions; how duplicate rows for one account in one extract are resolved; what happens to usage that arrives before its account (an inferred member) and when the real attributes arrive; and how usage facts are joined to the right version, by surrogate key fixed at load time or by business key and time at query time. Say which reports must show history as it was and which as it is now.
sections.constraints: For each account, versions never overlap and leave no gaps from the first version onwards. Re-running a day's load gives the same dimension. A month that finance has closed is not restated without a documented decision, even when a back-dated change says it was wrong. Every version records which extract produced it.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates and windows are hypothetical. Each account has a stable business key from the CRM. In this exercise a MERGE fails when more than one source row matches the same target row; check current docs for the exact behaviour.
sections.criteria: Tracked versus overwritten attributes chosen with reasons; surrogate key, business key and half-open validity interval with a no-overlap, no-gap invariant; a MERGE that closes and inserts in one statement from a deduplicated, change-detected source; back-dated changes that split intervals correctly; inferred members for early facts, completed later; an explicit choice between keys fixed at load and as-of joins, with cost; as-was versus as-is reporting and closed periods respected; idempotent loads with checks for one current row per account; each incident detected and repaired without editing history silently.

clarifications.q: Which attributes need history?
clarifications.a: Tier, segment, region and parent company. The account owner's email and phone are overwritten, never versioned.

clarifications.q: What does the extract say about time?
clarifications.a: Each row has an effective_date from the CRM and the file's extract time. A back-dated correction has an effective date in the past.

clarifications.q: How do I tell a real change from a re-sent row?
clarifications.a: Your choice: compare tracked attributes (a hash is fine) and say what happens when nothing changed.

clarifications.q: How fast do reports need new accounts?
clarifications.a: Usage for a new account must be counted the day it arrives, even if the account has no attributes yet.

clarifications.q: Who reads the dimension?
clarifications.a: Finance's monthly revenue by tier (as it was at the time), sales dashboards (by today's segment and owner) and ad-hoc analysts.

hints: A MERGE updates or inserts per matched row. To close a version and insert its successor in one statement, the source can carry each changed account twice: once to match and close the current row, once with a null key so it never matches and is inserted.
Deduplicate the extract to one row per account and effective date before the MERGE, with a deterministic tie-break, or the MERGE fails or picks arbitrarily.
A back-dated change splits one existing version into two and may change the end of the version before it. Write down the before-and-after intervals before writing SQL.
followups: Walk through one ordinary change: the dimension rows before, the source rows you build, the MERGE clauses, and the rows after.
A correction says an account moved to the enterprise tier 20 days ago; the dimension has two versions since then. Show the intervals before and after, and which usage facts change.
Usage arrives for an account the CRM has never sent. What row do you create, what key does the usage carry, and what happens when the real attributes arrive two days later?
Finance closed last month on the old tier. Sales wants the correction everywhere. What does each report show, and how is the difference explained?

At {{accounts}} accounts and {{usage_rows}} usage rows a day, what does a back-dated change cost if facts carry surrogate keys? Compare with joining by business key and time, and say what you would choose.

rules.ask: Finance's revenue by tier for March must not change when an account moves tier in May. With the tier overwritten, how do you answer March?
The extract has the same account twice with different tiers. What does your MERGE do, and what should it do?
A back-dated change creates a new version in the middle of history. Which usage facts now point at the wrong surrogate key, and how many rows is that at {{usage_rows}} a day?
Two loads run out of order after a retry. How do you make sure exactly one version per account is current, and how do you check it every day?
Is your interval closed or half-open, and what end value does the current row carry? Show the join predicate a usage row at midnight on a boundary day uses.

incidents: A CRM bulk edit re-sends {{daily_changes}} of accounts with only the owner's phone format changed. The load treats every row as a change, the dimension grows by millions of versions in a week, and dashboard joins slow down.

A back-dated tier correction {{backdate_days}} days old was applied by updating the tier on the current version. Finance's closed month and the sales dashboard now disagree, and nobody can say what the tier was when the invoice went out.
A retried load ran twice for the same extract after a partial failure; for some accounts two versions are marked current, and usage for those accounts is counted twice in revenue by tier.

templates.title: Governance model — catalogs, grants, row filters, column masks and what inheritance really grants
templates.subtopic: securable hierarchy, principals and nested groups, privilege inheritance, row filters and column masks, effective-access model

sections.scenario: An insurance group moves its analytics to a lakehouse with a central governance layer. Data is addressed by a three-level name (catalog, schema, table), and the hierarchy above a table is a catalog and a schema; in this exercise a privilege granted on a catalog or schema applies to every current and future object inside it, and reading a table needs a usage privilege on its catalog and schema plus a read privilege on the table (check current docs for the exact privilege names). The group has {{business_units}} business units, about {{tables}} tables and {{groups}} groups synchronised from the identity provider, nested several levels deep. Customer data is spread across {{regions}}: claims handlers may see only their region's policyholders, actuaries see all regions but with names, emails and national identifiers masked, and a fraud team needs the unmasked values for open investigations only. Auditors ask regularly: "who could read this column on this date, and why?"
sections.problem: Design two things. First, the governance layout: how catalogs and schemas are organised (by environment, business unit, data domain or sensitivity), how groups are designed so that grants stay few, where row filters and column masks are attached and how they decide (a mapping table, group membership, an attribute of the user), and who owns each level. Second, the data model that answers access questions: securables and their hierarchy, principals and nested group membership with history, grants with history, filters and masks with their versions, and a derived effective-access view that says, for a principal, table and column at a point in time, whether it can read, which rows, masked or not, and the chain of grants that explains it.
sections.constraints: Least privilege: nobody gets more than their role needs, and a new table must not become readable by a broad group unless that is intended. Every grant, revoke, membership change and policy change is recorded with who did it and when. The effective-access answer must be reproducible for any date in the last two years. The design must survive table renames and a table being dropped and recreated with the same name.
sections.assumptions: Counts and regions are hypothetical. Group membership changes arrive from the identity provider within an hour. A row filter and a column mask are functions attached to a table or column that run for every query; in this exercise a table has at most one row filter, and a column at most one mask.
sections.criteria: A catalog and schema layout with a clear axis and stated owners; groups designed around roles with few, deliberate grants; inheritance treated as a risk with broad grants only where safe; filters and masks driven by membership or mapping tables, versioned and reviewed; a model of securables (stable ids, not names), principals, nested membership with history, grants with history, and policy versions; an effective-access derivation with cycle handling, as-of reproducibility and an explanation chain; each incident detected, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a grant deny access?
clarifications.a: No. Grants only add access in this exercise; the restrictions come from row filters and column masks.

clarifications.q: Are groups nested?
clarifications.a: Yes, up to five levels, and cycles are not allowed but have happened in the identity provider's data.

clarifications.q: Who may grant?
clarifications.a: Owners of an object and principals with a manage privilege on it. Say who should own catalogs and schemas: people or groups.

clarifications.q: Do service principals for pipelines count?
clarifications.a: Yes. They read and write more data than any human; include them.

clarifications.q: What is a "read" for the auditors?
clarifications.a: Being able to run a query that returns the column's values unmasked. Being able to see that the table exists is not a read.

hints: Inheritance makes grants cheap and dangerous: a read grant on a schema covers tables created next year. Decide where broad grants are allowed (curated, non-sensitive schemas) and where grants are per table.
Make filters and masks decide on group membership or a mapping table rather than naming users, so that access changes are membership changes, which are already audited.
Effective access is a derived fact: expand nested groups (transitive closure, guarded against cycles), walk the securable hierarchy, and combine with filter and mask versions as of a time.
followups: A claims handler in one region is also put in a cross-region project group. Using your model, show whether they can now read other regions' claims, and why.
A data engineer creates a new table of raw call-centre transcripts in a schema where a large analyst group has a schema-level read grant. What happens, and what in your layout prevents it?
The auditor asks who could read national identifiers unmasked in the claims table on 3 March. Write the query against your model, including nested groups as they were that day.
A table is dropped and recreated with the same name. Do old grants apply to it? How does your model keep the history of the old table separate from the new one?
With {{groups}} groups nested five deep and {{tables}} tables, how big is the effective-access view, how do you compute it incrementally and how fresh must it be?

rules.ask: That grant also covers every table created in the catalog from now on. Which future table worries you most, and what stops it?
You built a view per region instead of a row filter. How many views is that across {{business_units}} business units, and how do you keep them from drifting when the base table changes?
Your mask names individual users. What happens when someone joins the fraud team, and where does that change get audited?
The identity provider produced a membership cycle. What does your expansion do, and how do you report it?
The table was renamed last month and recreated under the old name. Which identifier do your grant history and audit answers key on?

incidents: A team grants read on a whole catalog to a large analyst group to unblock a deadline. Three weeks later a new table of unmasked customer contact data lands in a schema of that catalog and, through nested membership, is readable by people in many of the {{groups}} groups.
The identity provider sync fails for a day. People who left the fraud team keep unmasked access, and the effective-access view, rebuilt from the stale membership, says nothing changed.

A row filter function is edited to fix a bug and for an afternoon returns every region's rows (here {{regions}}) to one region's claims handlers; the change was made by the table owner without review, and nobody can say afterwards which queries ran during the window.

templates.title: Workspace audit-log model — who read what, when and from where
templates.subtopic: audit event normalisation, identity and securable resolution, network context, retention and immutability

sections.scenario: A bank runs {{workspaces}} workspaces on a data and AI platform. The platform emits audit events for actions in each workspace and in the governance layer: sign-ins, notebook and query runs, table and credential requests, permission changes, cluster and job changes, file downloads and token creation. Each event is a JSON record with a service name, an action name, the identity that acted (a user or a service principal), a source IP address and user agent, request parameters, a result and a timestamp; in this exercise events are delivered to the bank's storage after a delay of {{delivery_delay}}, at least once, and the set of services and actions grows with each platform release (check current docs for the event schema and delivery options). About {{daily_events}} events arrive a day. The compliance team must answer, within a day of being asked: who read a given table or column during a period, everything a given person did before and after they left, every permission change on sensitive data, and every access from outside the bank's network. Regulation requires keeping the evidence for {{retention_years}} years and proving it was not altered.
sections.problem: Design the data model from raw audit events to the tables that answer those questions. Cover: the raw landing table (what is kept verbatim and why), the normalised event fact (grain, keys, the columns you extract and how you handle actions you do not recognise yet), how you resolve the identity (users renamed, deactivated, service principals, tokens), the object acted on (a stable id for a table even when it is renamed or recreated) and the network context (corporate ranges, VPN, cloud services, unknown); which event types count as reading data versus only looking at metadata; deduplication of redelivered events; partitioning and retention tiers for {{retention_years}} years; and how you prove the evidence is complete and unaltered.
sections.constraints: Raw events are never modified or deleted before the retention period ends; derived tables may be rebuilt. Every answer to compliance must be traceable to the raw events it came from. The model must cope with new action names without a code change, and must state what it cannot answer (for example, which rows a query returned). Personal data in request parameters (such as query text) is restricted to the compliance team.
sections.assumptions: Workspace counts, volumes, delays and retention are hypothetical. Each event has an id that identifies it across redeliveries. Directory data (people, their employment status, their groups) is available daily from the bank's identity provider.
sections.criteria: Raw events kept verbatim, immutable and provably complete (counts, hashes or object locks); a typed event fact at one row per event id with redelivery deduplication and a generic category for unknown actions; identity, object and network dimensions with history, resolved as of event time by stable ids; explicit evidence strength for "read" versus metadata; service principals attributed to accountable people; late events handled with labelled answers and reruns; retention tiers and access control on sensitive parameters; each incident detected, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a "table read" event mean rows were read?
clarifications.a: Not always. Some events show that metadata was fetched or that a short-lived credential was issued for the table's files. Say which you treat as evidence of reading and how you word the answer.

clarifications.q: Are service principals people?
clarifications.a: No, but a person can create or use one. Say how you attribute a job's reads to the person accountable for it.

clarifications.q: How late can events be?
clarifications.a: Usually {{delivery_delay}}; rarely a few days during an outage. Say how an answer for yesterday is labelled.

clarifications.q: Can the bank alter events?
clarifications.a: Its engineers can technically delete files in its storage. Part of the design is making that detectable or impossible.

clarifications.q: Which IP ranges are internal?
clarifications.a: A list maintained by the network team, which changes. Answers about last year must use last year's list.

hints: Keep the raw event verbatim (with its arrival file and time) and derive a narrow, typed fact; unknown actions still land in the fact with a generic category, so nothing is lost when the platform adds actions.
Resolve identities and objects through dimensions with history (as of the event time), keyed by stable ids, not by names that change.
A "who read X" answer is a union over several action types with different strengths of evidence. Model the strength explicitly.
followups: Define the grain and key of the normalised event fact, and the deduplication rule for redelivered events.
Write the query for "who read the claims table between 1 and 31 March", including reads by jobs running as service principals and the table's earlier name.
A contractor's account is deactivated. List what you would show about their last 30 days, and which of those events are evidence of data access.
The network team reclassifies a range from "VPN" to "public cloud" in May. What happens to answers about April, and how does your model make that reproducible?

At {{daily_events}} events a day for {{retention_years}} years, estimate storage, describe the hot and cold tiers, and explain how you would prove to an auditor that no raw file was deleted or changed.

rules.ask: An auditor asks for every access from outside the corporate network last quarter. Which columns does that query read, and how long does it take across {{daily_events}} events a day if everything stays inside the JSON?
The person changed their name and email when they married, and later left. How does your model find all their events under both identities?
