Which tables may ever delete data before {{retention_years}} years, and how does anyone prove later that the raw events were not touched?
A nightly job running as a service principal read the table. Who does your answer name, and on what evidence?
Is the network classification looked up at query time or stored with the event? What does each choice do to an answer about last year?

incidents: A platform release renames one action used for table credential requests. For two weeks the normalised fact files it under "unknown", and the monthly "who read sensitive tables" report silently drops a third of its rows.

A delivery outage delays three days of events; they then arrive all at once, on top of the normal delay ({{delivery_delay}}). The compliance answer already sent for those days said "no access", and it was wrong.

An engineer cleaning up storage costs runs a retention job on the raw audit location with the derived tables' 90-day setting. Eight months of raw events are deleted before anyone notices, inside the {{retention_years}}-year obligation.

templates.title: Data quality expectations — failing rows, quarantined rows and the run-over-run trend
templates.subtopic: pipeline event log, versioned expectation actions, distinct counting, LAG over filtered runs

sections.scenario: A team runs declarative pipelines that build silver tables from clickstream data. Each dataset declares data quality expectations (named constraints such as non_null_user_id), each with an action: warn keeps a failing row and records the failure, drop removes the row (in this exercise the team routes dropped rows to a quarantine table) and fail stops the update. Each pipeline run, called an update, reads rows_in rows; every failed check is logged to expectation_failures with the record it concerns. {{status_rule}} {{version_rule}} {{log_rule}} The team wants one report that shows, per update, how bad the data was and whether it is getting worse.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns dataset, update_id, rows_in, failing_rows, quarantined_rows, failure_pct, prev_failure_pct, change_pts: one row per COMPLETED update, ordered by dataset, then started_at. failing_rows is the number of distinct records with at least one failed expectation in that update. quarantined_rows is the number of distinct records with at least one failed expectation whose action, in the version in force for that update, is drop. failure_pct is ROUND(100.0 * failing_rows / rows_in, 2). prev_failure_pct is the failure_pct of the same dataset's previous COMPLETED update (by started_at), NULL for its first one, and change_pts is failure_pct − prev_failure_pct (NULL when there is no previous one). An update with no failures appears with zeros.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Updates that did not complete are neither reported nor used as the previous update. The sample has {{updates}} updates, {{versions}} expectation versions and {{failures}} failure rows; production has thousands of pipelines and billions of failure rows a month.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, datasets, expectations and counts. Every expectation that appears in a failure row has a version in force for that update. An update's started_at is unique within its dataset.
sections.criteria: Completed updates as the driving set with a LEFT JOIN so clean updates show zeros; distinct records counted, not checks; the action resolved per update from the version in force at started_at (inclusive), not the current version or the log time; one drop failure enough to quarantine; LAG over completed updates only; deterministic ordering; can discuss like-for-like trends, alert rules and pre-aggregating the failure log.

clarifications.q: A record fails non_null_user_id and valid_country_code. How many failing rows is that?
clarifications.a: One. It is one record; it failed two checks.

clarifications.q: A record fails a warn expectation and a drop expectation. Is it quarantined?
clarifications.a: Yes. One drop failure is enough.

clarifications.q: Should a failed update count as the previous update?
clarifications.a: No. The trend compares completed updates only.

clarifications.q: Which action applies if an expectation changed from warn to drop?
clarifications.a: The version in force for the update, as the description states; the current version is not necessarily that one.

clarifications.q: Does ended_at matter?
clarifications.a: No. Use status and started_at.

hints: Start from the completed updates and LEFT JOIN the failures; an inner join loses the clean updates.

For each failed check, find the action in force for its update: the version with the latest effective_from at or before the update's started_at (a correlated subquery with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1, or DISTINCT ON, or a window over versions).
Filter to completed updates before LAG, so the window only sees completed updates; COUNT(DISTINCT …) FILTER (WHERE …) gives both counts in one pass.
followups: A new expectation is added and the failure rate jumps. How would you change the trend so that it compares like with like?
Alert when change_pts exceeds a threshold for two completed updates in a row. Write the extra step.
The failure log grows by billions of rows a month. How would you store and pre-aggregate it so this report reads megabytes, not terabytes?
A drop expectation removed 30% of rows in one update and the gold tables looked normal. Which numbers in this report should have paged someone, and who?

rules.ask: A record that fails two expectations: how many times does your count include it, and is that a failing row or a failed check?
Which updates disappear with an inner join between updates and failures, and are they the good news or the bad news?
Does your LAG run before or after you filter out failed and cancelled updates? What does it return for the update right after a failed one?
Is that the version in force now, or when the update started? Show the predicate that picks the right one.
Why might the time a failure was logged be the wrong time to look up the action? Which time decides the action for the whole update?

incidents: An expectation was switched from warn to drop on a Friday. On Monday this report showed a quarantine spike for the previous week's updates, because an earlier version of the query joined the current action instead of the version in force.

A pipeline restart redelivered part of the event log. A dashboard that counted failure rows instead of distinct records showed the failure rate doubling for a few updates and paged the on-call engineer at night.

templates.title: Table-format transaction log at scale
templates.subtopic: optimistic concurrency, conflict detection, checkpoints, log and file cleanup

sections.scenario: A lakehouse platform manages {{tables}} tables for its customers. Each table is a directory of immutable data files in cloud object storage plus a transaction log: an ordered sequence of numbered commits, each listing the files it adds and removes along with schema and table-property changes. A table's state at version N is the result of replaying commits 0 to N. Many writers act on one table at once: streaming appends, MERGE statements that rewrite the files holding matched rows, deletes for privacy requests, and maintenance jobs that compact small files. The busiest tables take up to {{commits}} commits a minute. Readers, including time-travel queries to older versions, must always see a consistent snapshot.
sections.problem: Design the transaction log and its commit protocol. Cover how a writer commits atomically on object storage, how concurrent writers are detected and either reconciled or rejected, what a reader does to build a snapshot quickly (checkpoints every {{checkpoint_every}} commits in this exercise), how idempotent streaming writes avoid committing the same batch twice, how old log entries and unreferenced data files are cleaned up while time travel stays available for {{retention_days}} days, and how file compaction coexists with writers that never stop.
sections.constraints: No central database may sit in the read path for data files; readers find everything from storage (plus, if you choose, a commit service). Data files are never modified in place. A commit must be all or nothing, and a reader must never see half of one. Writers run in many different clusters and can crash at any point. Snapshot construction for a reader should take seconds, not minutes, even on the busiest tables.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and rates are hypothetical. The object store offers strongly consistent reads after writes and listing by prefix; whether it offers an atomic "create only if absent" write is a question you should ask.
sections.criteria: Commit = atomic creation of the next numbered log entry, with data files written beforehand and invisible until referenced; a mutual-exclusion mechanism per storage (conditional put, or a commit coordinator where the store lacks one) used by every writer of a table; conflict detection based on what the losing writer read and wrote (blind appends rarely conflict; a MERGE conflicts when a concurrent commit removed files it read or added rows matching its predicate), with retry without rewriting data when there is no logical conflict; checkpoints at a fixed interval with a validity check and a latest-checkpoint pointer; idempotent streaming commits keyed by application id and batch version; cleanup bounded by retention and by live readers; compaction marked as not changing data and scheduled or scoped so it can make progress; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does the object store support "put if absent"?
clarifications.a: Assume one cloud does and one does not. Say what you do on each.

clarifications.q: Which isolation level do writers need?
clarifications.a: Writes must be serialisable; snapshot isolation is acceptable for reads. Tell me where the two differ in your design.

clarifications.q: Can a compaction job change the data in a table?
clarifications.a: No. It rewrites the same rows into fewer files; readers of a change stream must be able to tell that nothing changed.

clarifications.q: How long must old versions stay readable?
clarifications.a: {{retention_days}} days, for time travel and audits. Older versions may be unavailable.

clarifications.q: Can a single commit be large?
clarifications.a: Yes: a MERGE can remove and add hundreds of thousands of files in one commit.

hints: Writers do their expensive work (writing data files) before they try to commit; the commit itself only has to win one atomic step on the next version number.
When a writer loses that race, it does not have to start over. Read what the winners changed and ask whether it conflicts with what this writer read and wrote.
A checkpoint is the replayed state at one version, stored so readers can start there; a pointer to the latest checkpoint saves a listing. Think about what happens if a checkpoint is half-written.
followups: Walk through two writers, a blind append and a MERGE, that both try to commit version 101 of the same table. Which succeeds, what does the other do, and when must the loser abort rather than retry?
How do you commit atomically on the cloud whose object store has no "create only if absent"? What fails if two clusters use different mechanisms for the same table?
A streaming job crashes after its commit succeeds but before it records its progress. How does the restarted job avoid writing the batch twice?
Which data files may cleanup delete, and how do you protect a reader that is still working on a snapshot from an hour ago?
On the busiest tables, compaction loses every conflict to the streaming MERGE and never finishes. How do you change the protocol or the scheduling so both make progress?

rules.ask: Where is the lock held, and for how long? A MERGE that rewrites files for twenty minutes would block a writer committing {{commits}} times a minute.
A writer loses the race for the next version. What exactly does it check against the winners' commits before retrying, and when does it have to rewrite its data files instead of only re-committing?
The writer producing a checkpoint crashes halfway through writing it. How does a reader know not to trust the partial checkpoint, and what does it use instead?
Which files are safe to delete, judged by what? How do you protect a long query or a time-travel read that started before cleanup ran?
Compaction and a streaming MERGE touch the same partition every minute. Which should win a conflict, and how do you stop the loser from starving?

incidents: A streaming MERGE commits into the busiest table up to {{commits}} times a minute. The nightly compaction of that table has failed with conflicts five nights in a row, the table now holds 900,000 files under 1 MB, and query planning on it takes over a minute.

Checkpoint writing for one busy table has failed silently for three days after a permissions change on its log directory. The data is still correct, but every new reader replays every commit written in those three days instead of at most {{checkpoint_every}}, and snapshot construction takes several minutes.

A cleanup job is run with a retention of one hour instead of {{retention_days}} days. A long-running report query and a time-travel audit query both fail with "file not found", and an auditor asks whether last week's version can still be reproduced.

After a storage migration, two writers on different clusters both report that they committed version 51,204 of a table. One writer's rows are missing from every reader's view, and its job reported success.

templates.title: Cluster autoscaling and spot-capacity fallback for many tenants' jobs
templates.subtopic: autoscaling, spot instances, quotas, fairness across tenants

sections.scenario: A managed data platform runs Spark clusters on cloud virtual machines for {{tenants}} customer workspaces. Each cluster has a driver and a variable number of worker nodes; jobs range from five-minute SQL transformations to twelve-hour shuffle-heavy backfills. At peak the platform runs about {{peak_nodes}} nodes in a region. To lower customers' bills, about {{spot_share}} of worker capacity runs on spot (preemptible) instances, which the cloud can reclaim with {{notice}} of notice; the rest is on-demand. Customers choose a minimum and maximum number of workers per cluster and expect jobs to finish on time at the lowest cost.
sections.problem: Design the autoscaling and capacity system: how each cluster decides to grow or shrink, how worker nodes are acquired across spot and on-demand capacity and across zones and instance types, what happens to a running job when spot nodes are reclaimed, how the platform shares cloud quotas and API rate limits fairly among tenants, and what you measure to show customers that autoscaling saved money without missing deadlines.
sections.constraints: Cloud APIs for launching instances are rate-limited per account and region, and instance quotas per type are finite. A lost worker loses the shuffle files and cached blocks it held unless they were moved first. Drivers must not be lost mid-job. One tenant's burst must not delay other tenants' scheduled jobs beyond their start-time targets. Launching a node takes one to four minutes.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, prices and timings are hypothetical. The reclaim notice of {{notice}} is this exercise's rule; real notice periods differ by cloud, so check current docs.
sections.criteria: Per-cluster scaling on workload signals (pending tasks and backlog, expected stage duration) with hysteresis, cooldowns and min/max bounds; scale-down that prefers workers without shuffle or cached data, or migrates it first; drivers on on-demand by default; a capacity broker that diversifies spot across instance types and zones, tracks reclaim rates, and falls back to on-demand by job deadline and cost; reclaim handling (stop scheduling on the node, migrate shuffle blocks within the notice, recompute what is lost, and checkpoint long lineages); fair sharing of quotas and launch rates with priorities for scheduled production jobs, jittered starts and retry budgets; cost and deadline reporting per job; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: What signal says a cluster needs more workers?
clarifications.a: You decide. The engine exposes pending tasks per stage, task durations and executor utilisation.

clarifications.q: Can the driver run on spot?
clarifications.a: Customers may ask for it; the default you choose must be defensible.

clarifications.q: Are tenants billed for the nodes their clusters use?
clarifications.a: Yes, per node-time at a rate that depends on instance type and spot or on-demand.

clarifications.q: Can jobs be moved to another zone after they start?
clarifications.a: Not the running cluster, but new nodes can come from any zone in the region if the job's storage and network allow it.

clarifications.q: Is there a pool of pre-started nodes?
clarifications.a: You may propose one; say who pays for idle capacity.

hints: Separate the per-cluster decision (how many workers does this job need now) from the regional decision (where those nodes come from, and in what order tenants get them).
Removing a worker is not free in Spark: it may hold shuffle output that later stages will read. Scale down the workers whose loss costs least, or move their data first.
A reclaim notice is a short window to act in. Decide in advance what a worker does with it.
followups: Walk through one cluster on a shuffle-heavy job: when does it add workers, when does it remove them, and what keeps it from oscillating?
Spot capacity for the cluster's instance type runs out in its zone. What does the system try next, in what order, and when does it fall back to on-demand?
A spot worker receives its reclaim notice mid-stage. What happens to its running tasks, its shuffle files and its cached data?
How do you share the region's instance quota and launch-rate limit among {{tenants}} workspaces so a large backfill cannot starve scheduled production jobs?
How do you show a customer, with numbers, that spot plus autoscaling saved money on their job, and what do you do when it did not?

rules.ask: CPU is low while a stage waits on a shuffle fetch, and high during a skewed stage running on one core. Is CPU the right signal for adding workers? What would you use instead?
A reclaim wave takes most of one zone's spot capacity in ten minutes. What do your running jobs lose, and what does it cost compared with running them on-demand?
With {{notice}} of notice, how much shuffle data can a worker actually move? What happens to the data that does not make it?
Which tenant waits when the quota is exhausted, and how does a scheduled job's start-time target enter that decision?
Who pays for the idle nodes in the pool, and how do you size it so the cost does not exceed the minutes it saves?

incidents: In one zone the cloud reclaims about 40% of spot capacity within ten minutes, with {{notice}} of notice per node. Long shuffle-heavy jobs lose map outputs, recompute stages repeatedly, and several run four times longer than usual while costing more than on-demand nodes would have.

At midnight UTC thousands of scheduled jobs from different workspaces start together. The cloud's rate limit for launching instances is hit, launches fail, and the platform's own retries keep the limit saturated for 25 minutes.
The autoscaler removes workers that look idle but hold shuffle files. The next stage fails to fetch them, recomputes, and the cluster scales up again; it oscillates every few minutes for hours.
One workspace submits a backfill of 6,000 jobs that takes most of the region's quota for the most popular instance type. Other workspaces' scheduled jobs wait more than an hour to start.

templates.title: Column-level lineage and catalogue service built from query plans
templates.subtopic: column lineage from plans, impact analysis, tag propagation, governed visibility

sources: SQL warehouses, notebooks, scheduled jobs and streaming pipelines

sections.scenario: A lakehouse platform's governance catalogue already lists catalogs, schemas, tables, columns and grants for {{tables}} tables. Customers want column-level lineage: for any column, which columns it was computed from and which columns, dashboards and models read it, captured automatically from the {{queries}} queries and job runs a day that execute in {{sources}}. They want impact analysis before changing a column, sensitivity tags (such as "contains personal data") that follow data downstream, and they want lineage to respect permissions: a user should not learn the names of tables they are not allowed to see.
sections.problem: Design the lineage service: where lineage is captured (from the engine's resolved query plan), the model for nodes and edges (including the kind of dependency), how SQL, DataFrame code, views, MERGE, streaming queries and user-defined functions are handled, the storage and query path for upstream and downstream traversals, how tags propagate, how visibility is enforced, and how fresh lineage must be. New lineage should be queryable within {{freshness}} of the query that produced it.
sections.constraints: Capture must not slow down customer queries or fail them if the lineage service is down. Tables are renamed, dropped and recreated with the same name. Some transformations are opaque (Python and Scala functions, external tools writing files directly). Traversals over popular shared tables can fan out to tens of thousands of downstream columns. Lineage is kept for one year.
sections.assumptions: All volumes are hypothetical. The engine can emit, for each executed write or read, its resolved plan: the input tables and columns (with stable table identifiers), the output table and columns, and the expressions connecting them.
sections.criteria: Capture from the resolved plan, asynchronous and fail-open with a durable buffer; nodes keyed by stable ids with names as time-versioned attributes; edges with kinds (value, filter/join, opaque) and validity intervals; explicit handling of MERGE, views, streaming and opaque functions (conservative all-inputs-to-output edges marked opaque); a storage model that serves bounded traversals (adjacency by node with pagination, precomputed table-level summaries, depth limits); tag propagation rules by edge kind with owner review for opaque edges; visibility enforced at query time with redacted placeholders; freshness measured and surfaced so "no readers" is never claimed from stale data; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do read-only queries create lineage?
clarifications.a: Reads matter for impact analysis (who reads this column), but they have no output table. Decide how you record them.

clarifications.q: Is a column used only in a filter or a join key a dependency?
clarifications.a: Customers want to know, but separately from columns whose values flow into the output.

clarifications.q: What about SELECT *?
clarifications.a: The resolved plan has already expanded it into specific columns.

clarifications.q: Do tags propagate automatically, or only suggest?
clarifications.a: Your call. Say what happens when propagation is wrong in either direction.

clarifications.q: Who may see a lineage edge?
clarifications.a: Anyone may see nodes they have access to; you must decide what they see for nodes they cannot access.

hints: Capture at the resolved plan, where names, * and views are already resolved, and ship the result asynchronously, so capture can never fail a query.
Key nodes by stable identifiers, not by names; a name is an attribute that changes over time.
Edges carry a kind (value flows from, filtered by, joined on, opaque) and a validity period, so the graph answers "what reads this column today" and "what read it last March".
followups: Show the edges you would emit for a MERGE that updates three columns from a joined source with a filter on a fourth.
How do you represent a Python function that takes three columns and returns one, when you cannot see inside it?
A downstream traversal from a widely used customer dimension returns 40,000 columns. How do you make it fast and useful?
How do you show lineage to a user who can see the start and end of a path but not a table in the middle?
A tag propagates "personal data" to a column that does not contain any, and data owners start ignoring tags. How do you make propagation trustworthy?

rules.ask: Your downstream query from one popular table touches tens of thousands of nodes. How do you bound that traversal, and what do you precompute?
Parsing SQL text misses views, *, DataFrame code and session settings. Why not capture the plan the engine has already resolved?
A table is dropped and recreated with the same name and a new schema. Does its new lineage join the old table's history?
An email column passes through that function into a shared table. What does your tag propagation do with it?
A user cannot see a table in the middle of a path. What exactly do you show them, and what can they infer from it?

incidents: A team drops a gold table and recreates it with the same name and a different schema. The lineage graph now attaches the new table's columns to the old table's upstream history, and an impact report lists 40 downstream dashboards that no longer read it.

An email column flows through a Python function into a derived table. The function is opaque to the plan, the personal-data tag never propagates, and the derived table is shared with an analytics group without masking.

After a spike in query volume, the lineage event backlog reaches six hours against a {{freshness}} target. During that window an engineer renames a column, checks impact analysis, sees "no downstream readers", and breaks 30 dashboards.
A user without access to a finance schema opens the lineage of a shared dimension and sees the names of finance tables and columns that read from it.

templates.title: Multi-task job orchestration with retries and repair runs
templates.subtopic: DAG scheduling, exactly-once runs, repair, shared compute

sections.scenario: A data platform lets customers define jobs as graphs of up to {{tasks}} tasks: notebooks, SQL queries, Python packages and pipeline updates, with dependencies, conditions ("run only if the previous task's value is true"), per-task retries (up to {{retries}}), timeouts, and parameters passed from one task to the next. Tasks can share one job cluster or each use their own. The platform runs {{jobs}} scheduled jobs; at the top of each hour about {{peak_starts}} runs start within a minute. When a run fails, customers can launch a repair run that re-runs only the failed tasks and the tasks that depend on them, reusing the results of tasks that succeeded.
sections.problem: Design the orchestrator: the job and run model, the scheduler that starts runs on time, the state machine for runs and tasks, dispatch to clusters, retries and timeouts, repair runs, shared job clusters, concurrency limits, and how the orchestrator itself stays available. Say what guarantee you give that a scheduled run starts exactly once, and what a task must do so a retry does no harm.
sections.constraints: The scheduler must survive the loss of any single machine without missing or duplicating a scheduled run. A run's history (every attempt, its parameters, cluster, start and end) is kept for 60 days. The orchestrator does not see inside tasks; it only knows start, success, failure, timeout and any values a task publishes. Starts may be at most one minute late at peak.
sections.assumptions: All volumes are hypothetical. Clusters take one to four minutes to start, and the cluster service has its own rate limits.
sections.criteria: Runs identified by (job, scheduled time) and created with a unique constraint or conditional write before any side effect; a partitioned scheduler (jobs sharded across instances with leases and fencing) that spreads the top-of-hour burst and survives failover without duplicates; a durable run/task state machine with conditional transitions; dispatch decoupled through queues with rate limits toward the cluster service; retries with backoff and jitter, timeouts with sensible defaults, and run and attempt ids passed to tasks for idempotent writes; repair runs as new attempts that reuse recorded outcomes, with a clear statement of what data a repaired task reads (or a parameter pinning the original logical date and table versions); containment for shared clusters; catch-up policies after outages with throttling; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can two runs of the same job overlap?
clarifications.a: The customer sets a maximum number of concurrent runs per job; the default is one.

clarifications.q: What does a repair run reuse?
clarifications.a: The successful tasks' recorded outcomes and published values from the original run. It cannot reuse anything a task wrote to a table; that data may have changed since.

clarifications.q: Who makes a task idempotent?
clarifications.a: The task's author, but the orchestrator can help by passing run and attempt identifiers. Say how.

clarifications.q: If a scheduled time is missed during an outage, should the run still happen?
clarifications.a: Customers want to choose: catch up every missed run, run only the latest, or skip.

hints: Make "this scheduled run exists" a durable, unique fact before anything starts. A run is identified by (job, scheduled time), not by the scheduler instance that noticed it.
Keep the run and task state machine in one durable store, with conditional transitions, so two schedulers or two workers can never both move a task from pending to running.
A repair run is a new attempt inside the same run, not a new run: it needs the original run's parameters and the outcomes of the tasks it skips.
followups: Walk through the scheduler at the top of the hour. How do {{peak_starts}} runs start within a minute, and what stops two scheduler instances from starting the same one?
A task fails on its last retry. What does the run look like, and what exactly does a repair run do with the tasks before it, after it and beside it?
Several tasks share one job cluster. One of them crashes the cluster's driver. What happens to the others, and how should retries behave?
How does a task that appends to a table make its retries and repairs harmless, and what does the orchestrator give it to help?
A region is down for two hours. When it returns, what runs, in what order, and how do you avoid a thundering herd?

rules.ask: Two scheduler instances both believe they own 01:00. What makes exactly one run exist for each job at that time?
The task already wrote half its output before failing. What does the retry find, and whose job is it to make that safe?
The repair runs two days later. The task before it succeeded, but its output table has been overwritten by later runs since. Which data does the repaired task read?
One task's memory blow-up takes down the shared cluster. How do you contain the damage, and do the other tasks' retries count against their limit?
What is the default timeout when the customer sets none, and who notices a task that has been running for fourteen hours?

incidents: The scheduler leader fails twenty seconds into the top-of-hour burst of {{peak_starts}} run starts. The standby takes over and starts again about a quarter of the runs the old leader had already started; jobs that append to tables load the same hour twice.

On Thursday a customer launches a repair for Tuesday's failed run. It re-runs the failed task and its dependents, but they read the upstream table as it is on Thursday, so Tuesday's report contains Wednesday's rows.

On a shared job cluster used by all {{tasks}} tasks of one job, a single task exhausts the driver's memory. Every running task fails at the same moment; their retries start together, on a new cluster, and fail the same way until all {{retries}} retries are spent.

A task waits forever on an external API and has no timeout. It holds the job's cluster for fourteen hours; the job's downstream deadline is missed, and the cost appears on the customer's bill before anyone notices.

templates.title: Vector search index kept in sync with lakehouse tables
templates.subtopic: incremental embeddings from a change feed, deletes, model versions, index health

sections.scenario: Customers of a lakehouse platform build retrieval-augmented applications over their own tables: support articles, product descriptions, contract clauses. They want a vector search index that stays in sync with a source table of {{rows}} rows without writing their own pipeline. About {{changes}} of the rows are inserted, updated or deleted each day. Each indexed row stores a {{dims}}-dimension embedding computed by an embedding model endpoint, plus the row's key and a few filterable columns. Applications expect search results to reflect a change in the table within {{freshness}}, and a deleted row must stop appearing in results.
sections.problem: Design the sync and serving system: how changes are read from the source table, how embeddings are computed and paid for, how inserts, updates and deletes reach the index, how the index records which table version it reflects, how an embedding model upgrade is rolled out, how access control on the source table applies to search results, and how you measure freshness, recall and cost.
sections.constraints: The embedding endpoint has a throughput limit and a cost per token. The table format provides a change feed: row-level inserts, updates (with before and after images) and deletes, each tagged with the commit version that made it. Some customers apply row filters to the source table, and search must never return a row the caller could not read from the table. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes degrade as rows are updated and deleted in place.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates and costs are hypothetical. The change feed is enabled on the source table, and its retention is long enough for normal sync but not unlimited.
sections.criteria: Incremental sync from the change feed with a durable checkpoint of source versions and idempotent upserts by primary key; the index records the source version it reflects and exposes freshness; embedding only when embedded columns change (content hash), with batching, rate limiting and cost tracking; deletes on a fast path (tombstone plus query-time exclusion) independent of the embedding backlog; model upgrades as a new index built side by side and switched atomically, never mixing spaces; row-level access applied at query time with over-fetching or pre-filtered search; recall and latency monitored against exact search on samples, with compaction or rebuild of index segments; protection against accidental full rewrites (detect unchanged content by hash before embedding); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does every update need a new embedding?
clarifications.a: Only if a column that feeds the embedding changed. Updates to other columns may change only filter columns.

clarifications.q: How are deletes handled in the index?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say how quickly a deleted row disappears from results and how.

clarifications.q: Can the whole index be rebuilt?
clarifications.a: Yes, but at {{rows}} rows a full re-embedding costs real money and takes time; say when you would do it.

clarifications.q: What if the change feed for a version range has expired before the sync reads it?
clarifications.a: Then incremental sync is impossible for that range; say what you do.

hints: Treat the sync like any incremental pipeline: a checkpoint of the last source version applied, idempotent upserts keyed by the row's primary key, and a record of which version the index reflects.
Separate what needs the embedding model (new or changed text) from what does not (deletes, filter-column updates). Deletes should never wait behind the embedding queue.
A model upgrade changes the vector space. Vectors from two models must never be compared with each other.
followups: Walk through one update to a row's text column: what the change feed shows, what you embed, and what the index holds at each step.
A deletion request removes a row from the source table. How quickly does it disappear from search, even when the embedding queue is a day behind?
How do you roll out a new embedding model over {{rows}} rows without a period where results mix two vector spaces?
A customer applies a row filter to the source table so each region sees only its own rows. How does search respect it?
Recall slowly drops as the index ages. How do you detect it, and what maintenance keeps it up without downtime?

rules.ask: At {{rows}} rows and {{dims}} dimensions, what does a full re-embedding cost in time and endpoint capacity, and what do applications see while it runs?
How long can a tombstoned row stay in the index, and what guarantees it never appears in a result in the meantime?
Updates and deletes accumulate in that index for months. What happens to recall and latency, and how would you know?
How large are your embedding batches, and how do you keep a backlog from breaking the {{freshness}} target without overrunning the endpoint's limit?
Do you filter before or after the nearest-neighbour search? What happens to the top ten when the filter removes nine of them?

incidents: The embedding endpoint is throttled to half its usual rate for a day. The backlog grows far past the {{freshness}} target, and a row removed from the source table for a customer's deletion request is still returned by search 30 hours later.

An engineer rewrites the source table with a full overwrite to fix one column. The change feed reports every one of the {{rows}} rows as deleted and re-inserted, and the sync starts re-embedding all of them at full cost.
An embedding model upgrade is rolled out by re-embedding rows only as they change. Three weeks later the index holds vectors from two models, and relevance has dropped for every query.
After months of updates and deletes, recall at 10 measured against exact search on a sample has fallen from 0.95 to 0.80, and p99 query latency has doubled.

templates.title: A large customer's jobs got slower after a platform upgrade
templates.subtopic: performance regression, communication under scrutiny

change: a new default for automatic shuffle partition sizing
a new query-optimiser rule turned on by default
a changed default for how files are sized on write
watching: the customer's head of data engineering wants a daily call with you
the customer's CTO has escalated to your executives
the customer's engineers have described the slowdown in a public community forum

sections.scenario: You are a senior engineer on the team that ships the managed runtime of a data platform: the Spark-based engine version customers' jobs run on. Two weeks ago a runtime upgrade rolled out to all customers; among many changes it included {{change}}. A large customer reports that {{jobs}} of their nightly jobs are now {{slowdown}}, and their morning reports are late. Your support organisation has made you the technical lead for the investigation, and {{watching}}.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead it: what you do in the first hour, the first day and the following weeks; how you mitigate before you know the root cause; how you find the cause; what you tell the customer, when and how; and what changes so the next upgrade does not do this to anyone. Then tell me about a real time you led an investigation while a customer or stakeholder was watching closely, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You may not read the customer's data without their written permission; you can see the telemetry the platform collects (query plans, stage metrics, cluster configuration). The upgrade includes security fixes, so rolling back every customer is not an option. Commercial matters (credits, contract terms) belong to the account team, not to you.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Mitigates before diagnosing (a scoped pin or setting change with the security trade-off made explicit and agreed); sets a communication rhythm with honest status and kept timing promises; investigates with evidence (before/after plans and stage metrics, a reproduction on synthetic or permitted data, bisecting the upgrade's changes); respects data-access boundaries; checks for other affected customers; decides the default with data from the whole fleet and the right owners; prevention through workload-representative regression testing and staged rollouts with per-change switches; real example with personal actions and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can one customer's workloads be pinned to the previous runtime?
clarifications.a: Yes, per workspace or per job, for a limited time, with the security trade-off made explicit.

clarifications.q: Is the change named in the release notes?
clarifications.a: Yes, in one line among forty.

clarifications.q: Have other customers complained?
clarifications.a: Two small ones filed tickets about "slower jobs" that nobody has linked to the upgrade yet.

clarifications.q: Does the customer have a test environment?
clarifications.a: They have one, with much less data.

hints: Mitigate first: a per-job or per-workspace pin, or turning one setting back, can restore the reports tonight while you investigate.
Compare the same job before and after the upgrade at the stage level; the plans and the stage metrics usually point at the change.
Decide what you will say and when you will next update before the first call, and keep every promise about timing.
followups: What happens in the first hour, and what do you say on the first call when you do not yet know the cause?
How do you find which of the upgrade's changes caused the slowdown, using only the telemetry you are allowed to see?
The customer asks you to promise this will never happen again. What do you say?
You find the change helps most customers and hurts this customer's job shape. What do you decide for the default, and who else needs to agree?
In your real example, what did you tell the stakeholder that you would say differently now?

rules.ask: The upgrade carries security fixes. Who decides whether this customer may run without them, and for how long?
Tonight's reports will be late again while you look for the cause. What do you do before you know it?
You have not been given permission to read their data. What can you learn from plans and metrics alone, and how would you ask for more?
That belongs to the account team. What do you give them so they can decide?
Which call did you personally make, and what did it risk?

templates.title: A breaking change in an open format that customers rely on
templates.subtopic: protocol upgrades, defaults, migration paths

feature: a row-level delete marker that avoids rewriting whole files on every delete
a column-mapping mode that allows renaming and dropping columns without rewriting data
a new statistics layout that makes file skipping far more effective

sections.scenario: Your team maintains a data platform's support for an open table format that many customers also read with other engines and older clients. The format records which features each table uses; a reader that does not support one of them must refuse to read the table rather than read it wrongly, so turning a feature on can lock out older readers. A new feature, {{feature}}, brings customers large benefits. Product wants it on by default for new and existing tables in {{months}} months. Platform telemetry suggests that about {{old_readers}} of customers' active tables are also read by at least one engine or client version that does not support the feature yet.
sections.problem: How do you decide what ships and how? Cover what you find out first, what compatibility promise the platform should make and write down, whether the feature is on by default for new tables, existing tables or neither, how customers are told and how they opt in or out, what happens to a table whose old reader breaks after the change, and how you bring product, the open-source community and customer-facing teams to one plan. Then tell me about a real time you shipped or blocked a change that was incompatible for some users, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Enabling the feature on a table is not trivially reversible. Other engines are maintained by other organisations, on their own release schedules. Product's date is tied to a public announcement.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. How a given format version handles feature flags and downgrades is this exercise's rule; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Gathers evidence first (who reads which tables with what; the blind spot of direct storage reads; downgrade feasibility); separates new tables, existing tables and shared tables; proposes a written compatibility policy (deprecation windows, explicit enablement, a documented downgrade path, release gates); communicates early with clear guidance and tools (a checker that lists a table's readers, opt-out settings); works with the open-source community and other engines rather than around them; plans the response for broken readers; reaches one plan with product without hiding the trade-off; real example with impact and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How good is the telemetry on old readers?
clarifications.a: It sees reads that go through the platform and some reads by other engines through its catalogue; reads directly from storage are invisible.

clarifications.q: Can a table be downgraded after the feature is on?
clarifications.a: Only by a maintenance operation that rewrites or cleans up data and then drops the feature; it takes time and may not be possible for every feature.

clarifications.q: Do other engines plan to support the feature?
clarifications.a: Some have it on their roadmap; dates are not committed.

clarifications.q: Who owns the announcement?
clarifications.a: Product marketing, with product management; your team owns the technical plan.

hints: The {{old_readers}} figure is a lower bound; ask what you cannot see before you decide anything.
New tables, existing tables and tables shared with others are three different decisions.
A compatibility promise is only useful if it is written down, specific and checked automatically before a change ships.
followups: What would you need to know before you agree to any default, and how would you get it within two weeks?
Product says opt-in means nobody will use the feature. How do you respond?
A customer's external reporting tool stops reading their tables the morning after the change. What happens next, hour by hour?
What compatibility promise would you propose for the format's features, and how would you enforce it in your release process?
In your real example, who was hurt by the change, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: For existing tables, who exactly gets the feature on that day, and how did you decide that their readers can handle it?
Reads directly from storage are invisible to your telemetry. How do you account for readers you cannot see?
Product says adoption will stall. What would make opt-in succeed, and how long would you wait before reconsidering?
Other engines release on their own schedule. What can you do to help them support the feature sooner, and what can you not control?
What was your own position, and did it change? Why?

templates.title: Growing a strong senior engineer toward staff
templates.subtopic: scope, influence, written design, honest feedback

area: the table-maintenance service that compacts and cleans up customers' tables
the query-planning layer of the SQL engine
gap: designs that are excellent but never written down, so other teams cannot build on them
deep work inside the team's own component, with little influence on neighbouring teams
strong opinions that win arguments but leave peers unconvinced

sections.scenario: You are a staff engineer on a data platform. A senior engineer who owns {{area}} has asked you to help them reach staff level within {{months}} months. Their technical work is consistently strong. Their last review named one gap: {{gap}}. Their manager supports the goal and has asked you to mentor them; promotion is decided by a group that reviews written evidence of impact.
sections.problem: How would you help? Cover how you would assess where they are, how you would agree on what "staff" means for them in concrete terms, what opportunities you would find or create, how you would give feedback, including uncomfortable feedback, what you would do as a sponsor rather than a mentor, and what happens if they are not ready at the end of {{months}} months. Then tell me about a real person you helped grow, with what changed for them, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You are not their manager. There is no staff-sized project waiting to be handed out. Your own roadmap does not get lighter.
sections.assumptions: The situation is hypothetical, and nothing here describes how any company runs promotions.
sections.criteria: Starts by understanding the person (their goals, their view of the gap, examples); turns "staff" into concrete, observable expectations agreed with them and their manager; chooses a real cross-team problem with visible stakes and sets them up to lead it; gives specific, timely, honest feedback, including about {{gap}}; acts as a sponsor (opens doors, credits them in writing, steps back so they lead); tracks progress with evidence; handles "not ready" honestly with a plan; real example with what changed for the person and the candidate's own contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does the engineer agree with the review's gap?
clarifications.a: Partly. They think the work should speak for itself.

clarifications.q: Are there cross-team problems they could take on?
clarifications.a: Several, unowned: inconsistent table-maintenance settings across teams, flaky end-to-end tests, an incident pattern that keeps recurring.

clarifications.q: How often can you meet?
clarifications.a: Every two weeks for an hour, plus whatever you arrange around real work.

hints: Make the expectation concrete: which problems a staff engineer here owns, and what evidence would show it.
The fastest growth comes from a real, cross-team problem with visible stakes, not from extra assignments.
Sponsorship is spending your own credibility: putting their name forward, and giving them the room to lead where you would normally lead.
followups: What do you do in your first two conversations, and what do you agree to measure?
Which cross-team problem would you steer them toward, and why that one?
Three months in, their design document for that problem is technically right and nobody has read it. What do you do?
At the end of {{months}} months you believe they are not ready. How do you tell them, and what happens next?
In your real example, what feedback did you give that was hardest to say, and what did it change?

rules.ask: That builds skill. What will you do that changes how others see their impact, and what does it cost you?
Give me the exact words you would use about {{gap}}, and what you would do if they disagreed.
Who owns that problem today, and how do you give it to them without taking it from someone else or setting them up to fail?
If the promotion does not happen at the end, what has the engineer still gained, and how do you keep them motivated?
What did you personally do or say?

templates.title: Negotiating reliability capacity against a feature-packed roadmap
templates.subtopic: reliability investment, evidence, error budgets

service: the catalogue service that every query consults for table metadata and permissions
the job scheduler that starts customers' workflows
launch: a new serverless compute option to be announced at a conference
a data-sharing feature promised to several large customers
an integration with a managed vector search product

sections.scenario: Your team owns {{service}} for a data platform. Last quarter it caused {{incidents}} customer-facing incidents; each one was fixed, and each fix was local. You believe the service needs {{ask}} of the team's capacity for the next two quarters to fix structural causes: a single database that every request depends on, retries that amplify overload, and missing load isolation between large and small customers. The roadmap is already full, and the product leader has committed the team to {{launch}}.
sections.problem: How do you get the time, or decide you should not? Cover how you build the case, what evidence you bring, how you size and sequence the work, what you offer product in exchange, how you keep the launch on track if the work happens, and what you do if the answer is no. Then tell me about a real time you negotiated capacity for reliability or technical debt against feature work, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot hire this half. The launch date is public. The product leader is measured on the launch; you are measured on both.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Builds the case from evidence (incident analysis showing shared structural causes, customer and business impact, load projections including the launch); frames reliability as part of the launch's success; sizes and sequences the work into milestones with measurable outcomes; offers real options with costs and lets the decision makers choose with the trade-off visible; uses or proposes an agreed objective and error-budget policy; plans for a "no" (mitigations, risk register, readiness for launch week) without sulking or sabotage; real example with outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are there written objectives for the service?
clarifications.a: An availability target exists; latency has none.

clarifications.q: Did the incidents breach the availability target?
clarifications.a: Two did, and the quarter's budget is spent.

clarifications.q: Does the launch depend on the service?
clarifications.a: Yes; the launch will add load to it.

clarifications.q: Who decides?
clarifications.a: The product leader and your engineering director together.

hints: Translate incidents into what product cares about: customers affected, hours lost, support load, deals at risk, and the launch's own risk.
Show that the launch adds load to a service that is already failing; reliability work may be part of the launch, not a competitor to it.
Offer options with costs: the full ask, a smaller first slice with explicit milestones, and doing nothing with its expected incidents.
followups: What does your one-page case contain, and what numbers are on it?
How would you sequence the {{ask}}, and what will be measurably better after the first six weeks?
The product leader offers 10%. What do you do?
The answer is no, and the next incident happens during the launch week. What do you do that week, and afterwards?
In your real example, what evidence changed the decision, and was the investment worth it?

rules.ask: The budget is already spent. What does your policy say happens now, and did product agree to that policy before this conversation?
Product hears "debt" as "engineers want to tidy up". How do you describe this work in terms of customers and the launch?
Your director and the product leader decide together. What do you bring to them so the choice is fair to both sides?
Each incident was fixed locally. What evidence shows they share a structural cause?
Which part of that case did you build yourself, and which argument did you lose?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a multi-cloud lakehouse
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, scaling across clouds and regions

angle: the storage layout and table design
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
cloud_feature: data residency, with some tables kept in one region
one access-control model across every cloud
a fixed budget for cross-cloud egress charges
disaster recovery to a different cloud

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if it ran as a lakehouse across {{clouds}} clouds, with tables stored as open-format files in each cloud's object storage and a requirement for {{cloud_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes across {{clouds}} clouds with {{cloud_feature}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The multi-cloud setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to layouts, keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible multi-cloud analysis that starts from data location, names single-cloud assumptions, and addresses {{cloud_feature}} incrementally (for example a single source of truth per table with replicas or shares, governance defined once and enforced in each cloud, compute placed next to data, tested failover); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a lakehouse or a Spark system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the multi-cloud part is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to file layouts, keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.

followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design assume one cloud or one region, and which would break first across {{clouds}} clouds?
How would you meet the requirement for {{cloud_feature}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Which copy is the source of truth, how far behind can the others be, and what does a reader in the other cloud see while a write is half replicated?
Put a number on it: how many bytes a day would cross between clouds in your design, and what would that cost?
